Mirror the struct layout and set restype/argtypes so values marshal correctly. import ctypes, sys lib = ctypes.CDLL("./libaacomm.so") # "aacomm.dll" on Windows, "libaacomm.dylib" on macOS class AacommConnection(ctypes.Structure): _fields_ = [ ("channel_type", ctypes.c_int32), ("controller_type", ctypes.c_int32), ("ip1", ctypes.c_int32), ("ip2", ctypes.c_int32), ("ip3", ctypes.c_int32), ("ip4", ctypes.c_int32), ("port", ctypes.c_int32), ("can_channel", ctypes.c_int32), ("can_baud_rate", ctypes.c_int32), ("can_send_address", ctypes.c_int32), ("can_receive_address", ctypes.c_int32), ("rs232_baud_rate", ctypes.c_int32), ("rs232_port_name", ctypes.c_char * 32), ] lib.aacomm_create.argtypes = [ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_void_p)] lib.aacomm_send_receive.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_int32, ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_int32, ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int32), ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int32)] result = ctypes.c_int32(0) lib.aacomm_start_server(b"", ctypes.byref(result)) h = ctypes.c_void_p() lib.aacomm_create(ctypes.byref(h)) conn = AacommConnection() conn.channel_type = 2 # AACOMM_CHANNEL_ETHERNET conn.ip1, conn.ip2, conn.ip3, conn.ip4 = 172, 1, 1, 102 lib.aacomm_test_connection(h, ctypes.byref(conn), 0, ctypes.byref(result)) if lib.aacomm_connect(h, ctypes.byref(conn), ctypes.byref(result)) == 0 and result.value == 0: buf = ctypes.create_string_buffer(256) is_error, size = ctypes.c_int32(0), ctypes.c_int32(0) lib.aacomm_send_receive(h, b"APos", 2000, buf, 256, ctypes.byref(is_error), ctypes.byref(size)) print("APos ->", buf.value.decode(), "is_error", is_error.value) lib.aacomm_disconnect(h) lib.aacomm_destroy(h) To receive async replies, push messages, or error/long-operation events, declare the matching CFUNCTYPE and register it. Keep a Python reference to the CFUNCTYPE instance for as long as it can fire — if it is garbage-collected the library calls a freed trampoline: REPLY_CB = ctypes.CFUNCTYPE(None, ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_int32, ctypes.c_void_p) ERROR_CB = ctypes.CFUNCTYPE(None, ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_void_p) def _on_reply(reply, is_error, user): print("reply", reply.decode() if reply else "", "is_error", is_error) def _on_error(error, user): print("error", error.decode() if error else "") reply_cb, error_cb = REPLY_CB(_on_reply), ERROR_CB(_on_error) # keep these alive lib.aacomm_set_error_callback.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ERROR_CB, ctypes.c_void_p] lib.aacomm_send.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.c_int32, REPLY_CB, ctypes.c_void_p] lib.aacomm_set_error_callback(h, error_cb, None) lib.aacomm_send(h, b"APos", 2000, reply_cb, None) Core contracts Handle lifecycle aacomm_create(&h) writes an opaque handle and returns AACOMM_OK (or a negative status on failure); aacomm_destroy() disconnects and frees it. One handle owns at most one controller connection. For concurrent connections, create multiple handles. Handles come from a table that never reuses a value, so a stale or forged handle resolves to AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE rather than undefined behavior. The connect handshake (optional) aacomm_start_server(path, &result) — spawn or locate AACS. ""/NULL uses the default resolution (or an AACS that is already running); result is the ConnectResult. aacomm_test_connection(h, &conn, is_known_controller_type, &result) — probes the controller and, when is_known_controller_type == 0, writes the detected controller_type back into conn. aacomm_connect(h, &conn, &result) — consumes that controller_type. Passing a freshly zero-initialized struct straight to connect (skipping test_connection) yields result == AACOMM_RESULT_INVALID_CONTROLLER_TYPE — run test_connection first, or set controller_type yourself. For firmware or FPGA download, call aacomm_download_firmware / aacomm_download_fpga directly — each opens its own connection (the handle must be disconnected) and uses neither aacomm_connect nor aacomm_connect_silent. aacomm_download_user_program is the exception: it downloads over the handle's already-connected session (connect first — it takes no aacomm_connection and rejects a disconnected handle). aacomm_connect_silent is for connecting to a controller in boot mode for direct messaging, where the identity/about handshake aacomm_connect performs is unavailable. Fill aacomm_connection by zero-initializing then setting only your channel's fields — 0 means "library default" for everything except channel_type (always honored) and can_channel (0 is a valid CAN channel). The struct layout must match the header exactly. Synchronous vs asynchronous messaging aacomm_send_receive blocks for the reply, writes it into your buffer, and sets *is_error. Sync and async pipelines are independent — you may interleave them from any thread. aacomm_send returns immediately; the optional aacomm_reply_cb fires exactly once — with the reply, or with is_error = 1 if the session tears down (disconnect / fatal) before the reply arrives. A consumer waiting on the callback never waits forever. Strings: the two-call pattern Output strings are UTF-8. The output functions (aacomm_last_error, aacomm_last_reply, aacomm_send_receive) take a buffer/buffer_len plus an int32_t* out_required: call with buffer = NULL, buffer_len = 0 to learn the required size (including the NUL) via *out_required, allocate, then call again. The copy is truncated to fit on a character boundary (never inside a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence) and always NUL-terminated, so if *out_required > buffer_len the text was truncated — for aacomm_send_receive the full reply is cached, so re-fetch it with aacomm_last_reply (which does not re-send the command). out_required may be NULL if you don't need the size. Callbacks and threading The callbacks — reply (aacomm_send), error, push, push_bytes, longop_started, longop_ended — are invoked on the library's firing thread, never on your calling thread. Keep them short and thread-safe: marshal work to your own thread/queue rather than blocking inside the callback. Each takes an opaque void* user_data that is passed straight through. Precise firing thread per callback: Callback Set by Fires on Notes reply passed to aacomm_send a dispatcher thread fires exactly once per accepted aacomm_send (reply, or is_error = 1 terminal error on teardown); the receiver thread never invokes it error aacomm_set_error_callback the receiver thread, synchronously a slow handler stalls reply/push classification — off-load with your own queue push aacomm_set_push_callback the thread pool the push message's text form as a C string — empty for both push sources the protocol defines (printf, push events), whose DATA is binary push_bytes aacomm_set_push_bytes_callback the thread pool the push message's payload bytes as (const uint8_t* data, size_t len) — everything after the ASCII envelope header, exactly as AAComm's BinaryData holds it; not a C string (NULs and bytes above 0x7F preserved). On the binary IPC dialect, the only one carrying push events, the trailing > CR packet terminator is included (n records = 7 + 50n + 2 bytes). (NULL, 0) when the library has no payload to hand over — an empty DATA section, or a packet it could not parse. Fires beside push when both are set longop_started / longop_ended the matching setter the firing thread bracket a busy window (reset/save/load) The const char* passed to a callback — and the push_bytes data pointer — is owned by the library and valid only for the duration of the call — copy it if you need it later; do not free it. Re-entrancy: do not call aacomm_send_receive from inside a callback — it fails fast with an in-band error reply instead of blocking (from a reply callback it is rejected outright; by the time the error callback fires the connection is already torn down, so it reports not-connected). Issue follow-up traffic from your own thread. Registering or clearing callbacks from inside a callback is allowed. A registered callback may fire until you clear it (pass a NULL function pointer) or call aacomm_destroy — destroy delivers pending reply callbacks terminally (is_error = 1), waits (bounded, ~2 s) for in-flight callbacks to return, and guarantees no callback fires after it returns, so callback state may be freed as soon as destroy returns. Per-handle threading A handle is single-threaded by contract: make calls on a given handle from one thread at a time (concurrent calls on different handles are fine, and callbacks arrive on library threads regardless). The recovery/two-call state — aacomm_last_reply after aacomm_send_receive, aacomm_record_result after aacomm_record, aacomm_last_error after any failure — is cached per handle, so a concurrent call on the same handle overwrites it between your two calls. Timeouts Every timeout_ms accepts 0 or a negative value as "use the family default": Family timeout_ms > 0 0 / negative aacomm_send_receive / aacomm_send per-call override the per-message default aacomm_record wait-for-completion bound 10 000 ms aacomm_download_firmware / _fpga / _user_program completion bound 180 000 ms (3 min) Error handling Every function returns an aacomm_status (0 == OK; -1/-2/-3 are NULL-arg / bad-handle / exception). On an AACOMM_EXCEPTION the detail text is available via aacomm_last_error(h, ...). The domain outcome of a connect/test/send is the ConnectResult written to the out_result parameter — a separate axis from the status (see Status / result codes). Message-level errors are in-band: aacomm_send_receive returns AACOMM_OK with *is_error = 1 and the reply text carrying one of a closed prefix set — "ERR " (controller error), "BOOT ERR" (controller error in BOOT mode), "ERR Sync:" (client-side sync-pipeline error: Timeout / Session terminated / No reply / callback re-entry rejection), "PC Suite: ERR" (API-synthesized, e.g. PC Suite: ERR 4020 = not connected). Timeout semantics: a timeout that expires while the message is still queued behind a slower call returns ERR Sync: Timeout without sending the message and keeps the connection; a timeout after the message reached the wire returns the same text but disconnects the handle — subsequent calls report PC Suite: ERR 4020 until you reconnect. Status / result codes aacomm_status (the return value of every function) is the ABI axis: Status Value Meaning AACOMM_OK 0 The call ran; inspect the out-params for the domain result AACOMM_NULL_ARG -1 A required pointer argument was NULL AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE -2 The handle is zero, already destroyed, or not from aacomm_create AACOMM_EXCEPTION -3 A managed exception was caught — see aacomm_last_error ConnectResult (written to the out_result of connect/test/server functions) is the domain axis. The values below are the aacomm_connect_result enum from include/aacomm_enums.h (generated from the AAComm.Shared.ConnectResult C# enum — do not edit). 0 is success. Code Value Meaning AACOMM_RESULT_SUCCESS 0 Connected / tested / sent OK AACOMM_RESULT_AACOMM_SERVER_NOT_RUNNING 1 No AACS reachable — call aacomm_start_server first AACOMM_RESULT_CORRUPT_ABOUT_FILE 2 The controller's About data failed to parse, or its keyword count disagrees with AIdentity[21], on a fresh read AACOMM_RESULT_INVALID_CONNECTION_DATA 3 The aacomm_connection fields are invalid for the channel AACOMM_RESULT_ALREADY_CONNECTED 4 Handle is already connected — aacomm_disconnect first AACOMM_RESULT_REQUIRED_CONNECTION_UNAVAILABLE 5 The requested channel/resource is not available AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_IOOPERATION 6 Low-level I/O operation failed AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_SOCKET_CONNECT 7 Could not reach the controller (Ethernet socket connect failed) AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_OPEN_COMM_HANDLER 8 Could not open the comm handler AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_RS232_CLEAR_BUFFER 9 RS-232 buffer clear failed AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_CONTROLLER_IN_BOOT_MODE 10 Controller is in boot mode — a normal connect cannot complete its handshake. aacomm_connect_silent opens a boot-mode controller without the handshake; aacomm_download_firmware itself requires a DISCONNECTED handle (the engine opens its own connection) AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_CONTROLLER_TYPE 11 Controller type query/handshake failed AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_RS232_CABLE_TYPE 12 RS-232 cable-type check failed AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_CANDELAY 13 CAN delay/timing failure AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_IDENTITY 14 Controller identity query failed AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_ABOUT_DATA 15 "About" data query failed AACOMM_RESULT_INVALID_CONTROLLER_TYPE 16 controller_type not set (skipped test_connection), or mismatch AACOMM_RESULT_CANLIB_MISSING 17 CAN driver library (canlib) not present AACOMM_RESULT_FW_INFO_MISMATCH 18 Deprecated — connect does not return it; the value keeps its number AACOMM_RESULT_NO_ETHERNET_INTERFACES 19 No Ethernet interfaces found on the host AACOMM_RESULT_ETHERNET_INTERFACE_DISCONNECTED 20 The chosen Ethernet interface is disconnected AACOMM_RESULT_ETHERNET_INTERFACE_MISMATCH 21 Ethernet interface does not match the controller subnet AACOMM_RESULT_ETHERNET_INTERFACE_ABNORMAL 22 Ethernet interface is in an abnormal state AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_FW_INFO 23 Firmware-info query failed AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_MAC_ADDRESS 24 MAC-address query failed AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_USER_PROG_INFO 25 User-program-info query failed AACOMM_RESULT_SIM_NOT_ENABLED 26 Simulator channel requested but simulator is not enabled AACOMM_RESULT_SIM_ONLY_ONE_SUPPORTED 27 Only one simulator connection is supported AACOMM_RESULT_ETHERNET_FAIL_ARP 28 ARP resolution to the controller failed AACOMM_RESULT_INVALID_CANBAUD 29 Invalid CAN baud rate AACOMM_RESULT_OPEN_CHANNEL_TIMEOUT 30 Channel open timed out AACOMM_RESULT_INVALID_ABOUT_REPLY 31 Controller's "about" reply was invalid AACOMM_RESULT_AACOMM_SERVER_FAILED_TO_OPEN_PROPERLY 32 AACS started but did not initialize correctly AACOMM_RESULT_CHANNEL_IN_EXCLUSIVE_COMMS_MODE 33 Channel is held by another client in exclusive mode AACOMM_RESULT_DUPLICATE_USER_UNIT 34 Duplicate user-unit definition AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_SOCKET_CONNECT_TIMEOUT 35 Timed out connecting to AACS AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_SOCKET_CONNECT_FAIL 36 Socket connect to AACS failed AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_SOCKET_CONNECT_EXCEPTION 37 Exception while connecting to AACS AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_FILE_MISSING 38 AACS executable file is missing AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_PROCESS_START_FAIL 39 AACS process failed to start AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_PROCESS_START_EXCEPTION 40 Exception while starting the AACS process AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_RESOLVE_WRONG_OS 41 AACS resolution: wrong OS for the located binary AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_RESOLVE_PCSUITE_DIR_MISSING 42 AACS resolution: PCSuite directory missing AACOMM_RESULT_AACS_RESOLVE_FILE_MISSING 43 AACS resolution: resolved file missing AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_IDENTITY_INDEX 44 Identity index out of range AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_IDENTITY_PARSING 45 Identity reply could not be parsed AACOMM_RESULT_FAIL_ABOUT_IDENTITY_INDEX 46 "About" identity index out of range AACOMM_RESULT_SERVER_NOT_BINARY_CAPABLE 47 AACS is too old to negotiate the binary protocol AACOMM_RESULT_CANDEVICE_NOT_CONNECTED 48 Kvaser driver is installed but no physical CAN interface is connected (distinct from CANLIB_MISSING=17, where the driver itself is absent) AACOMM_RESULT_SIM_LAUNCH_FAILED 49 The managed firmware-sim channel could not launch its firmware_sim process AACOMM_RESULT_SIM_NO_PORT 50 The launched firmware_sim never announced its loopback port AACOMM_RESULT_SIM_EXE_NOT_FOUND 51 The managed firmware-sim channel's simulator executable path is empty or names no file on the AACS host AACOMM_RESULT_SIM_STARTER_PAR_MISSING 52 No starter.par next to the firmware_sim executable, so the sim's parameter file cannot be created Channel and long-operation enums aacomm_channel_type selects the transport in aacomm_connection.channel_type: Constant Value Transport AACOMM_CHANNEL_RS_232 0 RS-232 serial AACOMM_CHANNEL_CAN 1 CAN bus AACOMM_CHANNEL_ETHERNET 2 Ethernet AACOMM_CHANNEL_SIMULATOR 3 Legacy param-echo simulator (test harness only) AACOMM_CHANNEL_SIMULATION 4 Managed firmware-sim channel — the server launches a local firmware_sim process over loopback aacomm_long_operation_type is the op_type passed to the long-operation callbacks: Constant Value Operation AACOMM_LONGOP_RESET 0 Controller reset AACOMM_LONGOP_SAVE 1 Save parameters to flash AACOMM_LONGOP_LOAD 2 Load parameters AACOMM_LONGOP_SAVE_USER 3 Save user data AACOMM_LONGOP_EVENT_CORRECT 4 Event-correction operation API reference aacomm.h is the authoritative per-function reference (documented inline). At a glance: Group Functions ABI aacomm_abi_version Lifecycle aacomm_create, aacomm_destroy, aacomm_is_connected, aacomm_last_error Connection aacomm_start_server, aacomm_test_connection, aacomm_connect, aacomm_connect_silent, aacomm_disconnect, aacomm_close_server Synchronous aacomm_send_receive, aacomm_last_reply Async + events aacomm_send, aacomm_set_error_callback, aacomm_set_push_callback, aacomm_set_push_bytes_callback, aacomm_set_longop_started_callback, aacomm_set_longop_ended_callback Recording + firmware/FPGA/user-program aacomm_record, aacomm_record_result, aacomm_download_firmware, aacomm_download_fpga, aacomm_download_user_program User units aacomm_get_user_units_enabled, aacomm_set_user_units_enabled In every signature below, h is an aacomm_handle from aacomm_create. Every function returns an aacomm_status (0 == OK; -1/-2/-3 == NULL arg / bad handle / internal exception — see Status / result codes); domain results travel in out_* parameters. The library never takes ownership of buffers you pass in, and the const char* it hands to callbacks is valid only for the duration of the call. ABI versioning & stability int32_t aacomm_abi_version(void); The SDK carries two version numbers, for two different purposes: Package version — the SemVer of the aacomm.* library / Agito.AAComm.Native NuGet, version-locked to the managed Agito.AAComm ($(AACommVersion); the native package ships on its own release line off the back of each managed release — see the distribution note above). This is what you pin in a package reference; release history is in CHANGELOG.md (shipped in the C/C++ archive). aacomm_abi_version() — a soname-style breaking-generation number, the C-ABI contract. It is bumped only on a breaking change: a changed or removed export signature, a struct layout change, a callback-signature change, or changed status-code semantics. Additive changes — new exports, new enum values, new result codes — never bump it (they cannot break a compiled consumer). It returns its value directly (it cannot fail) and takes no handle; the same value is the AACOMM_ABI_VERSION macro in the generated aacomm_enums.h. Generation 1 is the first shipped ABI (pre-release increments carried no compatibility meaning and were reset). Consumer rule — exact-match gate. Call aacomm_abi_version() once at load and reject a library whose value does not equal AACOMM_ABI_VERSION from the headers your binding was built against — coherent with the bump policy, because the number only moves when your binary genuinely cannot run. The bundled Python binding does this automatically; the committed include/aacomm.abi.txt records the exact export surface and the callback typedef signatures for that generation. Always build against the aacomm.h that ships with the library you load. Compatibility. The native client, the native AACS daemon, and the language bindings ship together at one package version — run matching versions. aacomm_enums.h, aacomm.abi.txt, and the Python mirrors are generated from the C# source and CI diff-gated; aacomm.h itself is hand-maintained — the manifest diff is what forces it to be updated in review, and its callback typedefs are additionally machine-checked against CallbackAbi.Callbacks by the generator. Lifecycle int32_t aacomm_create(aacomm_handle* out_handle); Allocates a client session and writes its opaque handle to *out_handle. Returns AACOMM_OK, or AACOMM_NULL_ARG if out_handle is NULL / AACOMM_EXCEPTION on internal failure. Each handle owns one AAComm client (and thus at most one controller connection). Free every handle with aacomm_destroy. int32_t aacomm_destroy(aacomm_handle h); Disconnects (best-effort) and frees the handle and its client. Returns AACOMM_OK, or AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE if h is unknown/already freed. After this call the handle and any callbacks registered on it are invalid; do not reuse it. int32_t aacomm_is_connected(aacomm_handle h, int32_t* out_connected); Writes 1/0 (open controller connection?) to *out_connected. Returns AACOMM_OK, AACOMM_NULL_ARG (NULL out-param) or AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE. Does not allocate; safe to poll. Because the bad-handle case is a distinct status, out_connected == 0 unambiguously means "not connected" (not "bad handle"). int32_t aacomm_last_error(aacomm_handle h, char* buffer, int32_t buffer_len, int32_t* out_required); Copies the handle's most-recent error text (UTF-8, NUL-terminated) into buffer (two-call sizing; *out_required receives the required byte length including the NUL when non-NULL). Returns AACOMM_OK or AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE. The error text is set by the most recent operation that returned AACOMM_EXCEPTION on this handle. Connection int32_t aacomm_start_server(const char* exe_path, int32_t* out_result); Spawns or locates AACS (the shared AAComm server process). Pass "" or NULL for default resolution (or to attach to an AACS already running); exe_path may be a UTF-8 path to a specific AACommServer executable. Writes the ConnectResult to *out_result (0 == AACS is up; AACS-resolution/start codes are values 35–43). Returns AACOMM_OK/AACOMM_NULL_ARG/AACOMM_EXCEPTION. Process-wide, not per-handle — call it once before connecting. int32_t aacomm_test_connection(aacomm_handle h, aacomm_connection* conn, int32_t is_known_controller_type, int32_t* out_result); Probes the controller described by conn (non-const: when is_known_controller_type == 0 it detects the controller type and writes it back into conn->controller_type so a subsequent aacomm_connect can consume it — see the connect handshake). Pass non-zero only when you have already set controller_type yourself. Writes the ConnectResult to *out_result. Returns a status (AACOMM_NULL_ARG if conn/out_result is NULL, AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE for a bad handle). int32_t aacomm_connect(aacomm_handle h, const aacomm_connection* conn, int32_t* out_result); Opens the controller connection, querying identity / about / firmware data. Requires conn->controller_type to be set (run aacomm_test_connection first, or set it yourself) — otherwise *out_result == AACOMM_RESULT_INVALID_CONTROLLER_TYPE (16). Writes the ConnectResult to *out_result. int32_t aacomm_connect_silent(aacomm_handle h, const aacomm_connection* conn, int32_t* out_result); Opens the connection without querying the controller for identity/about/firmware data (it only clears the RS-232 buffer on a serial channel) — the path for connecting to a controller in boot mode, where the normal identity handshake is not available. (Firmware download has its own export, aacomm_download_firmware, which manages its connection internally — don't connect first.) Writes the ConnectResult to *out_result. int32_t aacomm_disconnect(aacomm_handle h); Closes the controller connection for the handle (the handle stays valid and can reconnect). Returns AACOMM_OK, AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE, or AACOMM_EXCEPTION. int32_t aacomm_close_server(aacomm_handle h, int32_t force); Closes the AACS process this client is using. force != 0 requests an unconditional shutdown; 0 is a cooperative close. Returns AACOMM_OK, AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE, or AACOMM_EXCEPTION. Pair it with aacomm_start_server when your program owns the AACS lifecycle. Synchronous messaging int32_t aacomm_send_receive(aacomm_handle h, const char* command, int32_t timeout_ms, char* reply_buf, int32_t reply_cap, int32_t* is_error, int32_t* out_required); Sends command (UTF-8) and blocks until the reply arrives. Writes the reply text (UTF-8, truncated to fit on a character boundary and always NUL-terminated) into reply_buf/reply_cap, sets *is_error to 0/1 (the controller/transport error flag; also 1 on internal failure) when non-NULL, and writes the full reply byte length including the NUL to *out_required when non-NULL (so *out_required > reply_cap means it was truncated — re-fetch with aacomm_last_reply). timeout_ms > 0 overrides the message's default. Returns AACOMM_OK, AACOMM_NULL_ARG (NULL command), AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE, or AACOMM_EXCEPTION. Sync and async pipelines are independent; this may be interleaved with aacomm_send from any thread, but must not be called from inside a reply callback. int32_t aacomm_last_reply(aacomm_handle h, char* buffer, int32_t buffer_len, int32_t* out_required); Re-fetches the reply from the most recent aacomm_send_receive on this handle (two-call UTF-8, same sizing rule as aacomm_last_error) without sending the command again. Use it when a prior aacomm_send_receive buffer was too small. Contiguous array download double values[] = { 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 }; aacomm_array_download_result result; int32_t status = aacomm_download_array_f64( h, "AGenData", 1, values, 4, 0, 60000, 0, &result); aacomm_supports_array_stream(h, &supported) answers whether stream transport is available. Ask it rather than timing a trial download: firmware that predates the feature answers message 0x04 through its ordinary command parser. Both array functions block for the final result. f64 accepts floating-point values; i64 preserves exact 64-bit integers. AAComm selects Zynq stream transport only when the controller and server advertise it, otherwise it falls back to legacy bulk/individual assignments. Controller and stream errors are returned in result with AACOMM_OK, and so is a download refused before anything was sent: AACOMM_ARRAY_REJECTED, with the refused element's index when the keyword table ruled it out. An ABI failure uses the negative function status and leaves result.status at AACOMM_ARRAY_COMMUNICATION_ERROR. Never blindly retry when result.outcome_known == 0. Asynchronous messaging + events int32_t aacomm_send(aacomm_handle h, const char* command, int32_t timeout_ms, aacomm_reply_cb reply_cb, void* user_data); Enqueues command (UTF-8) and returns immediately (AACOMM_OK on enqueue; AACOMM_NULL_ARG / AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE / AACOMM_EXCEPTION otherwise). If reply_cb is non-NULL it fires once when the reply arrives, as reply_cb(const char* reply, int32_t is_error, void* user_data); pass NULL to fire-and-forget. timeout_ms > 0 overrides the default. user_data is passed through verbatim. int32_t aacomm_set_error_callback(aacomm_handle h, aacomm_error_cb cb, void* user_data); int32_t aacomm_set_push_callback(aacomm_handle h, aacomm_push_cb cb, void* user_data); int32_t aacomm_set_push_bytes_callback(aacomm_handle h, aacomm_push_bytes_cb cb, void* user_data); int32_t aacomm_set_longop_started_callback(aacomm_handle h, aacomm_longop_started_cb cb, void* user_data); int32_t aacomm_set_longop_ended_callback(aacomm_handle h, aacomm_longop_ended_cb cb, void* user_data); Register (or, with a NULL cb, clear) a session-level event callback on the handle. Each returns AACOMM_OK or AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE. Only one callback of each kind is held per handle — a later registration replaces the earlier one. Callback signatures and firing threads are in Callbacks and threading; user_data is passed through verbatim to each invocation. aacomm_error_cb — void cb(const char* error, void* user_data) — fatal comms error. aacomm_push_cb — void cb(const char* message, void* user_data) — controller push message as a C string (its text form — empty for the binary-payload push sources). aacomm_push_bytes_cb — void cb(const uint8_t* data, size_t len, void* user_data) — the same push as its payload bytes, exactly as AAComm's BinaryData holds them (everything after the ASCII envelope header; on the binary IPC dialect that includes the trailing > CR packet terminator). Not a C string — NULs and bytes above 0x7F are preserved. (NULL, 0) when there is no payload to hand over: an empty DATA section, or a packet the library could not parse. Both push callbacks fire when both are registered. aacomm_longop_started_cb — void cb(int32_t op_type, void* user_data) — op_type is aacomm_long_operation_type. aacomm_longop_ended_cb — void cb(int32_t op_type, int32_t error_code, void* user_data) — error_code 0 means success. This surface is v0 and intentionally minimal — it will be extended as the SDK matures. Always build against the headers that ship with your library (the aacomm_connection layout in particular must match), and call aacomm_abi_version() to verify the loaded library matches the header you built against — the value is bumped on any breaking change. See also In the repo (AACommComponents/): AACommNative/packaging/README.md — building a library from source, per RID. AACommNative/sample/sample.c — a complete pure-C program (also in the sdk zip). AAComm/docs/native-aot-sdk.md — design, status, and roadmap.

articles/release-notes/aacomm-changelog..title: AAComm Changelog | Agito AAComm SDK
articles/release-notes/aacomm-changelog..summary: Changelog All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file. The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning. [15.0.0] - 2026-10-30 ⚠️ Breaking Server-side SimProfileWriter.DefaultText() no longer invents a48V supply; use its explicit-voltage overload or resolve a known product. A raw unidentified simulator requires an explicit valid vbus_v profile. MessageData.DynamicPtr is now a long (was int), so a 64-bit simulator's memory address fits. A consumer that reads the property into an int must widen it or use IsDynamicPtr, and a binary built against the old type must recompile. IsDynamicPtr is unchanged. A message that a closing session drops before sending it, and a SendReceive that races the close, now reply PC Suite: ERR 4025 (the connection closed before the message was sent) instead of PC Suite: ERR 4020. 4020 now means only that the API had no connection when the call was made. A consumer that read 4020 as a teardown also matches 4025, or tests the new AACommEventArgs.IsSessionClosed. The AssemblyVersion is pinned to 15.0.0.0 for the whole 15.x line (package and file version keep the full number). .NET Framework consumers must recompile against 15.0.0 — a binary built against 14.0.0.0 does not bind, and no binding redirect bridges the identity change. .NET 8/10 consumers see no difference. IIdentityContainer gains PushEventQueueDepth. A consumer that implements the interface itself must add the member (CS0535); a consumer that only reads the container sees a new property. ICommService gains both DownloadArray overloads. A consumer that implements the interface itself must add them (CS0535); a consumer that only calls it sees new members. CommAPI.MessagesInBulk reports the bulk capacity, 50, on a ChannelType.Simulation connection, as it does on Ethernet. The firmware-simulator channel has always carried a MessageType.BulkMessage, but the property said 1 there, so every consumer that routes on it took the one-message-per-command path: recording-parameter download (AACommDataRecManager.SendRecordingParams) on a Simulation connection now crosses as one bulk instead of one message per parameter, and the AAMotion parameter batches batch there too. A consumer that read MessagesInBulk == 1 as "not an Ethernet connection" now sees 50 on Simulation as well. AllStatInterpreter.ParseAllStatData now takes the AllStat reply as AAComm delivers it — the resolved text a caller reads from AACommEventArgs.MsgReceived — and reads those values straight into AllStatData. It used to expect the raw controller longs and re-run the IEEE 754 decode and the User Units factor itself, so the only reply a consumer can actually obtain was converted twice: on a controller with 64-bit AllStat every floating-point field came back 0. The structured data now carries exactly the values the reply text shows, already scaled. Callers pass the received reply unchanged — and must not ask for it with AACommMessage.SkipUserUnits, which suppresses the User Units factor but not the IEEE 754 decode, so it never yields raw wire values. Added CiFpgaFeatures.FromReadback decodes the remote FPGA capability snapshot that AGM800 and AGM800-EC firmware publish in CiIdentity[24..41]: the generation, the availability (CiFeatureAvailability) and the main and auxiliary index-output bits. A read that is not bracketed by a matching generation and availability, or whose header or check word is wrong, decodes as CiFpgaFeatures.Unknown Two ConnectResult codes name why a managed Simulation connection could not launch its firmware_sim: SimExeNotFound (51), when ConnectionData.SimExePath is empty or names no file on the AACommServer host, and SimStarterParMissing (52), when no starter.par is next to the simulator executable, as with a firmware_sim built from source rather than packaged. Every other launch failure is still SimLaunchFailed (49), with its cause in the AACommServer log. A client older than the server gets FailOpenCommHandler for the two new codes Add immutable verified event-table definitions and an explicit captured-session Load/Arm/Complete/Abort/acknowledgement client. Preparation validates and reads back all three raw columns/settings; ambiguous writes retain process-local ownership, and recovery never crosses to a replacement connection without retirement proof. EventTableStatusReader provides bounded live coherent status/error/capability observations over a captured connection; typed unsigned fields retain the firmware publication and error provenance. Cancellation abandons unsent reads without implying remote Abort. CommAPI.CaptureSession() binds a multi-request operation to its original connection, including disconnect/reconnect to the same endpoint. Its cancellation token and replies reject a closed session. Verified-table preload capability uses Identity[62] bit0x200; Central-i master keyword caches distinguish its presence without requiring manual cache deletion. SimParameterFile.Configure explicitly delivers a complete selected-motor agito.par and physical profile to a disconnected simulator's memory folder without deleting its user program. Fresh managed launches initialize from the packaged complete starter; reconnect keeps the saved parameter file. Managed firmware simulation writes an explicit product-specific supply into the motor profile and preserves caller voltage overrides. Unknown products require an explicit finite positive vbus_v; invalid or unresolved supplies fail before launch. SimSupplyVoltage.TryGet exposes verified nominal simulator supplies by product identity. Unknown products have no implicit supply; IsValid checks an explicit finite positive voltage. PassiveCollectionRequest.EncoderSelections opts individual mapping scopes into main or auxiliary absolute-encoder metadata. The passive collector reports table-approved configured type/bit widths, the controller's processed absolute value and raw main diagnostics, with device identity, qualified reported resolution, full health and query capability kept explicitly unavailable. Main and auxiliary scopes remain distinct, no controller settings or protocol queries are sent, and callers without selections retain their existing reads. AAComm.Commissioning is a portable result contract for discovery and commissioning passes: CommissioningReport records per-controller/remote-port/axis/encoder observations with value, units, origin (configured, declared, controller- or device-reported, measured, inferred), acquisition source, outcome and reason, capture time, and linked attempts and hash-referenced evidence, and CommissioningValidator.Validate rejects a report that contradicts itself (a configured value presented as device-reported, a failed or partial acquisition presented as a success, nonfinite or ambiguous values, dangling or cyclic derivations, a stored ComtStatus presented as fresh phasing, a failed restore recorded as completed). A clean validation says the report is consistent, not that any hardware state is true. PassiveMetadataCollector (AAComm.Commissioning) is the first producer of a CommissioningReport. Over an ICommService it records the identity the shared IIdentityContainer exposes (axis and motor-axis counts, capability flags, current-loop sample rate, recording limits), and for each caller-supplied port/axis/encoder mapping the configured EncType and the stored ComtStatus[1], using ordinary parameter reads only. Identity values are marked as cached at connect and stamped with the host time of collection; a collection is not an atomic snapshot. A disconnected service, an unloaded or lacking message table, a failed read, an unmapped or out-of-range axis, and the product, firmware, FPGA and serial-number fields the interface does not expose each stay an explicit outcome with a reason, never zero or false. Collect appends one attempt per call, so a repeat keeps earlier failures beside later successes. Nothing here changes aacomm.rig-manifest/1. AACommEventArgs.IsSessionClosed is true for a reply that ended because its session closed: ERR Sync: Session terminated for a message already sent, PC Suite: ERR 4025 for one never sent. A consumer can leave those to the one OnCommsError report of a lost connection instead of reporting each request. Error texts for the lock/event guards of Firmware-Main #1256, in English and Chinese: ERR 403 (a lock/event source change refused while Lock or Event is on, LockEventMode 1/2) and ERR 404 (Lock/Event refused, the offset is stale). LockEventWriteOrder (AAComm.Services) holds the write order a restore needs under those guards (Order, whose Plan.Added and Plan.Inits name the rows it adds), the dependency list (EncSinCosHWEn, EncDir, VEncSrc, VEncOn, AuxEncDir, VEncFact, VEncFactDen), ReadCurrentModes for the controller's current LockEventMode where the rows carry none, and Mode2Supported, read from LockEventMode's declared maximum: firmware that declares it up to 2 is the firmware with the guards, and only it needs the order. AGM800-EC enable (Firmware-Main #1258, merged as 5fa8dcc2a): every EtherCAT Enable Operation forces LockEventMode 2 (when it isn't 2 yet, the drive first turns LockEn/EventOn off, which also drops an armed touch probe), and, on an axis with an ancillary counter, waits for LockEventStat 1 before the motor turns on (an axis without one skips the wait). If the mode isn't taken, or the offset still isn't learned after 8 LockEventInit attempts, the axis faults with 0x603F = 0x7300. LockEventWriteOrder.EnableForcesMode2(productType, lockEventMode) (an AGM800-EC whose firmware declares LockEventMode up to 2) and EcEnableLockOffsetFault (0x7300) expose this. That forcing happens only at the next enable, so Order(rows, isSupported, currentMode) decides LockEventInit from the mode the axis is in when it re-arms (the file's LockEventMode row, else the controller's current mode from ReadCurrentModes), on an AGM800-EC too. The ERR 403 text (EN/ZH) and its explanation now also cover the firmware's refusal to enter LockEventMode 1/2 on an offset that moved since arming. MessageDataValueExtensions.UserUnitsValueStr(MessageData, double, UserUnitsData) formats a Min, Max or Default value in user units: the float format when the parameter is floating-point, when user units scale it, or when the value has a fraction. MessageData.GetDescription and the allowed range in a controller error message use it, so their text is unchanged. AACommRemoteFpgaInfo.AllowAga155CurrentRatingMismatch is a default-false engineering option for AGA155 2A06 ↔ 2A10 FPGA comparisons (identity current codes 6 ↔ 10). All other target checks remain; AllowForce keeps its separate unknown-identity behavior and cannot bypass known mismatches. The package now ships lib/netstandard2.0 alongside net48, net8.0 and net10.0. A project targeting netstandard2.0 can reference Agito.AAComm directly instead of building AAComm from source. Nothing changes for existing consumers: NuGet still resolves the closest-matching target, so a net48, net8.0 or net10.0 project gets exactly the assembly it got before. CommAPI.DownloadArray downloads a contiguous array from typed double or exact long values and returns an ArrayDownloadResult with the selected transport, the applied count and the count that reached the controller, first failed index, error code, and known/unknown outcome. On Ethernet it uses the Zynq 0x04 stream when both controller and AACommServer advertise support, otherwise it falls back to legacy bulk or individual writes. Timeouts and disconnects are never retried. A download refused before anything is sent ends as ArrayDownloadStatus.Rejected with the refusal's error code and a known outcome, nothing applied: AACommServer refused it (another client holds exclusive access, for one), or an element's index or value is outside the keyword's table, which FirstFailedIndex then names. A parameter the table refuses outright still throws ArgumentException. An element's error, on either transport, reads as one sentence in ErrorMessage: its index, the reply (ERR 14, or PC Suite: ERR 14 when refused before sending), the error's description and, for a value out of range, the keyword's allowed range. ArrayDownloadResult.StreamError reports the controller's array-stream protocol error as the ArrayStreamError enum (bad version, flags, width, count or index range; checksum mismatch; trailing data; unexpected reply), and ErrorMessage names it. A checksum mismatch is reported only after the controller has applied every element, so that result carries a full AppliedCount for a write whose integrity check failed — read the array back rather than trusting the count. CommAPI.SupportsArrayStreamDownload reports whether the connected controller and AACommServer both advertise stream transport. The controller advertises it in Identity[62] bit 0x80; do not probe by starting a download, which older firmware answers through its legacy command parser. The packet sniffer raises SnifferService.OnRetentionFailure (path, count) after 10 consecutive failed deletes during retention or byte-budget enforcement — a capture file held by antivirus or another process no longer fails silently forever. Capture continues; the count resets on the first successful delete. Push events. A controller push with SOURCE = 2 now reaches CommAPI.OnPushMessageReceived as an AACommPushMsgPushEvents — Missed, FreeRows, and Events, a list of PushEventRecord (Type, Axis, TimeSec, TimeTick, Data1..Data5; PushEventRecord.NoAxis marks a controller-wide event). PushSources.PushEvents names the source. A packet whose length does not match its record count, or whose VERSION_DATA is not 1, arrives as an AACommPushMsgError, as a malformed printf push does. Push events are binary-IPC-only: the bundled AACommServer never forwards a SOURCE = 2 push to a legacy string-protocol client, whose framing cannot carry a binary payload safely, so a consumer whose CommAPI.ServerCompat is LegacyAscii does not receive them. Printf pushes still reach both client kinds. The push-events capability and queue depth read from the controller Identity. ControllerIdentityFeature_02.PushEvents_Supported is Identity[62] bit 0x40 (the firmware's IDENTITY_NEW_FEATURES_2_PUSH_EVENTS), reachable through IIdentityContainer.Features_02; IIdentityContainer.PushEventQueueDepth is Identity[75], the depth of the controller's push-event queue — 64 on an AGM800, 0 on a firmware without push events, whose Identity array ends before index 75. Implementors of IIdentityContainer must add the PushEventQueueDepth member. The native C-ABI SDK gains a byte-safe, length-carrying push callback beside the const char* one: aacomm_set_push_bytes_callback / aacomm_push_bytes_cb deliver the push message's raw DATA payload as (const uint8_t* data, size_t len, void* user_data) — exactly the bytes AACommPushMsgBase.BinaryData holds, the binary IPC dialect's trailing >\r terminator included — so a SOURCE = 2 push-events packet — mostly zero bytes — reaches a C/C++ consumer intact, and aacommpy exposes it as Client.on_push_bytes. The existing aacomm_push_cb is unchanged; the addition is additive and the ABI generation stays 1. A new product type, AGM800-EC: ProductTypes.AGM800_EC_ID (16) and ProductTypes.AGM800_EC ("AGM800-EC"). It is the first product in both families: ProductTypes.IsAGM800 and ProductTypes.IsEtherCAT both return true for it, and so do ConnectionData.IsAGM800 and ConnectionData.IsEC on a connection to one. IdToName / NameToId resolve it. Its firmware image is its own, not the AGM800 one: AACommFwInfo.ValidateFwFiles refuses an AGM400 / AGM800 / Pulse-Sync .bin on an AGM800-EC connection and an AGM800-EC .bin on those — by the image's identity markers (with or without a .ver), and by the .ver Type: line, which must start with AGM800-EC on an AGM800-EC connection and must not on the others — and AACommFwInfo.ProductTypeStr reports "AGM800-EC" for its image. ControllerIdentityContainer.DefaultSamplingRate returns 16000 for it, the EtherCAT current-loop rate. AACommDownloadFW flashes an AGM800-EC's EtherCAT SII EEPROM when you pass AACommFwInfo.Targets.EC_ESI: the SII .bin goes down as Intel-HEX lines after DownloadESI, over Ethernet (or the firmware-sim ChannelType.Simulation channel), while the controller runs its firmware — it is refused in boot. The target is yours to pass: an AGM800-EC SII image and its firmware image are both .bin files, and AAComm does not recognize an SII image by its content, so with the default Legacy target an SII image is flashed as firmware. EC_ESI refuses a .hex, a .bin larger than the 16 KiB an ESI image can address (the AGM800-H1G's SII is 2 KB; a firmware image is megabytes), and a .bin carrying firmware identity markers, and on an AGM400, AGM800 or Pulse-Sync connection it is refused before anything is sent. Controller fault 1082 (CON_FLT_EXTERNAL_AMPLIFIER_FAULT, ADP05 / AGL105 with an external amplifier) has a description: "External amplifier fault (e.g. Varedan undervoltage)". Remote FPGA download supports 16K (10M16) devices: FlashSizes.Model16K (3), a .ver with FPGA Size: 16K is accepted, and the image is written to the 10M16 CFM0 base (0x12800), including the upper flash-address bits (register 0x30B). First used by ADP05 (AGL105). ConnectionData.SimMemoryFolder — opt-in absolute path of a folder a managed Simulation connection keeps its memory in. AACommServer creates it when missing, starts firmware_sim with it as its working directory, and never deletes it, so what the simulation saved to flash is still present on the next connect. The simulation writes its saved files there: a 5.3.0 AGM800 simulator writes its parameters to agito.par and its user program to agito.prg. Left empty (the default), every connect still gets a fresh scratch folder, saved files included, that is removed on disconnect. A relative path is refused with ConnectResult.SimLaunchFailed. ControllerIdentityVersions.BuildCiRemoteVersionString(ciIdentity4, ciIdentity15To19) returns a Ci remote unit's FPGA version text from CiIdentity[4] and CiIdentity[15-19]. A unit whose CiIdentity[4] is 4444 gets the five words formatted by BuildVersionString (so owner 0 with sub-version 2 reads 5.5.0-rc2, and a null or short word list gives an empty string); any other unit gets the old A.BBB text, always with a dot, whatever the machine's culture. aacomm.cli reads a remote unit's FPGA version through it. ControllerVersionWord is a public, comparable firmware or FPGA version word (Major.Minor.Patch plus owner and sub-version), built with FromWords from the five identity words or with TryParse from X.Y.Z, X.Y.Z-rcN, X.Y.Z.O or X.Y.Z.O-S. A release candidate orders below its final and a development build above it. ControllerIdentityVersions.FirmwareVersionWord returns the connected controller's firmware as one (null for the old firmware format and in boot mode). Changed When the packet sniffer is unavailable because Npcap is not installed, the AACommServer window and the AACommServerNative console now link to the Npcap download page, https://npcap.com/#download. Npcap is not redistributed with AAComm; install it yourself to use the sniffer. A ChannelType.Simulation connection starts its firmware_sim child with AGITO_DRAW_GCC set to %LOCALAPPDATA%\PCSuite\HostGcc\bin\gcc.exe when that file exists, so Draw runs on the simulation with the host compiler PCSuite downloads, whichever client started AACommServer. A value already set in AACommServer's environment is passed through unchanged. Simulation connections load their packaged or saved configuration without sending firmware requests during open. Saved motor types, including zero, and gains survive reconnect. Use Configure Motor or SimParameterFile.Configure for explicit reconfiguration. A firmware or FPGA download (AACommDownloadFW, AACommDownloadFPGA, AACommDownloadFPGARemote, AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat) now takes the channel's exclusive comms just before its single-client check and holds it until the download ends, and takes it again after each reconnect it makes. A client that calls CommAPI.Connect on the same channel during the download is refused with ConnectResult.ChannelInExclusiveCommsMode, and every message from another client (one connected with ConnectSilent included) is answered CHANNEL_IS_EXCLUSIVE, instead of interleaving with the flash. On an AACommServer older than 7.0.1 the lock is not taken and the download runs unprotected. A SendReceive whose timeout closes the connection now also raises CommAPI.OnCommsError (ERR Sync: Timeout (<message>)), on the calling thread before the call returns, so a consumer that follows the connection through the event learns of the disconnect. The call still returns ERR Sync: Timeout. A ChannelType.Simulation connection starts its firmware_sim child with AGITO_CI_REAL_AMP=1, so an AGM800 or AGM800-EC simulation drives its simulated remote amplifier: the axis phases, the encoder moves and the phase currents are live. The drive simulations ignore the variable. A value already set in AACommServer's environment is passed through unchanged, so AGITO_CI_REAL_AMP=0 keeps the stock simulated-amplifier path, where the axis arms but never moves. The embedded fallback message table, the catalogue in force before a controller's About is read, carries seven more rows (Print, ProgResetAll, PosKi, EmulRat, CurrAInTh, VelUnitFct, Speed), lifted from a real controller capture. In that window those mnemonics now resolve instead of reporting MnemonicNotFound, MessagesContainer.AllMnemonics counts 21 rows, and a .par upload started there lists the four writable ones. FPGA download no longer refuses every Ethernet address other than the factory default 172.1.1.101. The gate is now the same ARP guard the FW path runs: a non-default address is refused only while another device answers on the default one. A legacy (AGD200-class) FPGA download still reconnects at the default address mid-flow, so the default must be free on the subnet — which is exactly what the guard checks. A cached About table that no longer matches the controller is read again from the controller on Connect instead of failing with CorruptAboutFile, which now means the controller's own About data is inconsistent. ProductTypes.NameToId resolves either half of a paired product's name: AGD301 and AGC301 return AGD301_AGC301_ID (11), and AGD200 and AGC300 return AGD200_AGC300_ID (5), where they returned -1. AGD301 and AGD200 are how the firmware catalogue and PCSuite's Simulations\<product>\ folders name those products, so those names now resolve like every other product's. IdToName is unchanged and still reports AGD301orAGC301 / AGD200orAGC300. AACommServer extended Ethernet diagnostics summarize array-stream headers and cap raw packet previews at 64 bytes. Disabled extended logging no longer formats complete firmware or array payloads only to discard the result. The message that refuses a firmware download over CAN (AACommDownloadFW) no longer ties Ethernet to the AGM800: it reads Firmware download is not supported over CAN. Download firmware over Ethernet or RS-232 (serial). An exception thrown by an OnProcessEnded handler of AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat at the end of a download now propagates to the caller of StartDownloading, which runs the whole download on the calling thread; the handler is called once. ControllerIdentityVersions.BuildVersionString, and through it FirmwareVersionStr, FPGAVersionStr and CMFirmwareVersionStr, shows a release candidate (owner 0, sub-version N greater than 0) as X.Y.Z-rcN instead of X.Y.Z. AACommFwInfo.AACommVersionFromString follows: a .ver line 5.5.0.0-1 resolves to 5.5.0-rc1. A user program compiled on a release candidate carries that form in its FirmwareVersion: line, so it loads on that controller and not on its final; one compiled earlier carries X.Y.Z and must be recompiled. The About cache folder of a release candidate is named by the new form. FirmwareSystemVersion, IsFPGAVersionEqualOrGreater and the firmware-to-FPGA match check are unchanged. Fixed A late dispatcher or synchronous timeout from a closed session cannot send commands to, or disconnect, a replacement connection at the same endpoint. RS-232 decimal text replies, including 100000.0, retain their exact text through ASCII and binary IPC instead of becoming incorrect integers when their lengths match binary reply frames. Remote FPGA download verifies boot before erase/data writes and primary before success, including when the final reboot trigger returns ERR 151 after taking effect. The original error remains in status output; failed preparation, reconnect/readback, wrong images and ordinary flash errors still terminate without repeating the transfer or bypassing identity checks. Recording uploads reject nonempty payloads with no resolved vectors or an incomplete interleaved sample frame, reporting the observed scalar/vector counts instead of returning uneven vectors. Header-only inputs and complete stopped captures whose actual length differs from the requested length remain accepted; asynchronous and sequential uploads report the reason through OnError without a successful upload callback. The ERR 412 description writes the PDSubType input type as C0/C1 (zero), as the firmware names it, instead of CO/C1. Connecting to a 64-bit Linux firmware simulator no longer fails with ConnectResult.CorruptAboutFile about half the time. The About table's DynamicPtr is a memory address, and when it landed above Int32.MaxValue its 32-bit parse threw, so the table load failed. A managed Simulation connection no longer shares its memory with every other connection that runs the same firmware_sim. AACommServer starts the simulation with AGITO_FLASH_FILE pointing into its working directory, the SimMemoryFolder when one is given, overriding a value in the server's own environment, so the parameters (agito.par) and user program (agito.prg) that a Save to Flash writes stay with that connection; without it the simulation kept them beside its own executable, so a Save to Flash on one connection appeared on the next connection to that simulation, whichever client opened it. ControllerErrorInterpreter.GetErrorCodeFromErrorString reads the code from the multi-line text GetFormattedErrorText builds ("ERR 21\nSent: ...\nError: ..."), and from any error text that continues after the code; it returned the unresolved code 4005 for those. An exception thrown by an AACommMessage.OnReplyReceived callback ends the process as an unhandled exception, as it did up to 12.x, after AAComm writes it, with its full stack trace, to a debug log snapshot under %LocalAppData%\PCSuite\AAComm_DebugLogs. From 13.0.0, which moved the callback onto the send dispatcher, it had been discarded without a trace, so a failing reply handler looked like a hang. A consumer whose handler can fail must catch inside it. On .NET 8 and .NET 10, a fast stream of received data no longer overflows the stack and ends the process: the AAComm client, AACommServerNative and an in-process AACommServerModel re-armed each socket receive from inside its own callback. A CommAPI.SendReceive that races a Disconnect returns the PC Suite: ERR 4020 reply, like any SendReceive on a disconnected channel. It used to throw ObjectDisposedException when the disconnect had already disposed the session it was about to use. A firmware download over Ethernet to a drive ends at once, with Failed sending Password. Reply: ERR <code>, when the controller refuses the first password. It used to reconnect for a boot that never started and report the refusal late (or as a timeout). A firmware download over Ethernet to a legacy drive stops waiting for the boot on the factory address 172.1.1.101 once 100 s have elapsed, checked before each probe, and then falls back to the address it started on. The wait was a fixed number of probes, so on a host where each took about 3 s the fallback ran late or never inside a caller's time budget (aacomm.cli flash reported did not complete within 300 s). The status line during that wait reads Reconnecting TCP/IP to <ip>... (Attempt <n>) with no total. An EtherCAT drive's ESI download (EC_ESI) refuses an image larger than 16 KiB before sending it: the image is written as Intel-HEX records from address 0xC000, so 16 KiB is all that can be addressed. A user-program download started from inside AACommDownloadUP.OnProcessEnded runs once, not twice. AACommExclusiveCommsManager kept one completion callback per instance, so a Start issued from that handler while the previous download's End was still in flight completed whichever callback was stored last, and the ending download's Stop reply started the next one a second time. Each Start and End now completes its own call's callback. Chained downloads — an N-iteration loop driven from OnProcessEnded — are the affected case; the synchronous form (a null onDone) and the public surface are unchanged. The About cache is kept per firmware build. Controllers that share a product and firmware version but differ in build or current rating keep separate cached About tables (ControllerMessagesList.<peakCL>.<count>.<fwinfo>.xml in the product/version folder), so connecting to one no longer discards the other's, and a drive's PeakCL / ContCL assignments are no longer range-checked against another rating's limits. The first Connect to each controller after upgrading reads its About data once; the files an older AAComm wrote in that folder are left in place for it. A product/version folder keeps the tables of the 8 builds most recently read from a controller; reading another deletes the oldest, and a controller of that build reads its About data again on its next Connect. Applications that connect at the same time to controllers of the same firmware build no longer corrupt or delete each other's cached About table. A freshly read table is written beside the cached one and moved into place only once it passes its keyword-count check, so a Connect never loads a half-written table, a table that fails the check (CorruptAboutFile) is discarded instead of replacing the cached one, and an About reply that fails to parse (FailAboutData) no longer leaves a partial table behind. XmlHandler opens its file with FileShare.Delete, so replacing a file another process is reading no longer fails. An About table whose MinValue, MaxValue or DefaultValue is not a finite number is refused on every target. The -nan a firmware can send for a floating-point parameter's limits loaded on .NET 8 and .NET 10 — the connect succeeded with NaN limits, and the cached About file kept them for every later connect over any transport — while .NET Framework already refused it; NaN and Infinity loaded on all three. Such a table now fails to load on every target, Connect reports CorruptAboutFile, and the load error names the parameter and the field. A firmware .hex written on Linux or macOS (LF record endings, as hex2000 emits there), or one whose records mix LF and CRLF endings, is now parsed and validated like one written on Windows; the identity block was only found behind CRLF, so such a file failed the pre-flight check, with a substring error or as a file carrying no identity data. A parameter file uploaded from a controller downloads back without range rejections on float parameters. A float parameter's reply carried the value at double precision — ATorqueConst read 9.9999997171806854E-10, the 17-digit form of the 1e-9 the controller actually holds — which lands fractionally below the keyword's declared minimum, so every such line came back AssignedValueOutOfRange (error 14) on download. An unscaled float parameter now reports in its own width (1E-09), which re-parses to the identical stored value. Reply text changes for every float parameter — .par files, Terminal output, anything reading a reply — and carries at most 9 significant digits instead of up to 17. Double parameters are unaffected, and a float value scaled by a User Units factor still reports the scaled value at double precision, where the extra digits carry the division back to the stored value. A float32 parameter assignment whose value sits on the parameter's own declared bound is accepted instead of being refused as out of range. The bounds were compared at double precision while the value that goes on the wire is a float32, so any 17-digit rendering of a value on a bound — the form every .par file written before the reply-width fix above carries — parsed as outside them. Both sides now compare at float32 width, so a file already written that way downloads without hand-editing. A recording-parameter download (AACommDataRecManager.SendRecordingParams, and the sync manager over it) whose bulk the controller answers with an error now reports that error through OnError instead of never completing. A bulk stops at the failing command, so its ERR nnn is the last segment of the reply and has no terminator after it; the reply parser sliced past the end of the text and threw inside the reply callback, so neither OnSendRecordingParams nor OnError fired and AACommDataRecManagerSync.SendRecordingParams waited forever. A controller-link failure no longer takes the bundled AACommServer down with it. A hardware fault ends the channel, and the server closed that channel's client IPC socket as part of the eviction, then read its own teardown as the client having died — so with a single client attached (the usual case) the server exited about five seconds later, while the client was still running. An application that reported the FATAL to its user and waited for them to reconnect found the server gone, and the reconnect failed with AACommServerNotRunning until it started a new one. The socket now survives the eviction, and a Close from a fatal-evicted client is read as the goodbye it is. The self-shutdown still fires when a last client dies without saying goodbye. The behavior lives in the bundled server, so client and sidecar move together: a client against an older AACommServer.exe still sees the old exit. ParamAbout reports the bounds of a SCALING parameter (InUserUnits 4 — StuckTime, InTargetTime, RptWait, MaxVBusTime, DualStuckTime and their siblings) in the unit the parameter reads in: divided once by the controller's scaling factor and truncated the way the parameter table's own bounds are, so the reply agrees with MessageData.MinValue / MaxValue / DefaultValue. It multiplied instead, so the min / max / default it returned for these were out by the square of the factor (a 250 ms StuckTime default came back as 67108.8671875). Live values were and are unaffected: the controller converts those itself. A printf push (SOURCE = 1) whose VERSION_DATA is not 1 now reaches CommAPI.OnPushMessageReceived as an AACommPushMsgError carrying a NotSupportedException, as a push-events packet at an unknown VERSION_DATA already does. It used to be parsed with the version-1 layout regardless, so a packet from a firmware with a newer printf format could arrive as a valid AACommPushMsgUP carrying wrong messages, or as an error only when its bytes happened not to fit. The bundled AACommServer frames the controller push socket per packet. TCP may deliver two push packets in one read, or one packet across two, and each read was forwarded as one push: a printf packet followed by a push-events packet in the same read lost the events, the reverse order lost both, and a packet split across two reads reached CommAPI.OnPushMessageReceived as an AACommPushMsgError, or as a truncated push followed by one. Every packet now arrives whole and on its own, and the string-client filter for SOURCE = 2 applies per packet. A push the server does not frame — anything but printf and push events at VERSION_DATA 1 — is still forwarded verbatim; a packet whose terminator is not where its header says is dropped by the server instead of forwarded, and after a drop each read that does not start with a printf or push-events envelope is forwarded verbatim, framing resuming at the first read that does. The framing lives in the bundled server, so client and sidecar move together. A controller-link FATAL tears down only the session it was raised for. The in-flight SendReceive is woken before the teardown runs, so a caller that treats that failure as expected and reconnects immediately could have its new session torn down by the old FATAL and see PC Suite: ERR 4020 on its next message — the EtherCAT firmware download hit this at the reconnect right after the password that drops the drive into BOOT, where it reconnects at the drive's own address within ~100 ms, and then succeeded on the retry because the drive was already in BOOT. OnCommsError is not raised for a FATAL whose session is already gone. A .ver version line written in the controller's own development form, 5.4.4.12-1 (ALPHA), is accepted by AACommFwInfo.AACommVersionFromString and by the FPGA-vs-FW restraint check (which compares its dotted head, 5.4.4.12), instead of throwing on the suffix. 5.4.4 and 5.4.4.12-1 resolve as before. An assignment to a parameter the firmware holds as an integer now crosses as an integer on the string transports too, rounded to-even in controller counts. Dividing a display value by the User Units factor rarely lands exactly on a count — 244.39 at 0.01 mm/count is 24438.999999999996 — and only the CCC frame builder rounded it, so the same command reached an RS-232 or Simulator controller one count short of what it carried over Ethernet. The transmit seam now rounds a ParamType 0 / 3 parameter in counts before rendering, matching CanMessageParser, and does so at factor 1 as well, so a fractional value written to an integral parameter no longer reaches a string-transport controller as a decimal it cannot hold. Float and double parameters keep their fraction, and a command the seam does not rewrite still crosses byte-for-byte. User Units scaling is now applied on the way out on every transport. A write only ever reached the scaler when it was built into a CAN frame, so the same assignment left in engineering units over RS-232, over a Simulator connection and as a single-command MessageType.EthernetASCII message while the reply came back scaled — a read-modify-write on those paths divided the value by the factor on each cycle. The division now happens above the transport branch, so an assignment reaches the controller in counts whichever channel and whichever IPC dialect carries it, and AACommMessage.SkipUserUnits suppresses it there just as it suppresses the receive factor. Firmware, user-program and CNC/SpecialBulk payloads stay raw in both directions, as before; bulk messages keep scaling per sub-message; an EthernetASCII body under one of the ASCII-bulk keys (L, I) carries a list this layer does not parse and stays raw as it always has. Existing callers that sent RS-232, Simulator or EthernetASCII assignments in controller counts while User Units were enabled must stop pre-dividing, or set SkipUserUnits. The API-only User Units config gate now fires on every transport too: a raw assignment to *UnitFct / *UnitUnt[] is rejected with error 4023 over RS-232, over a Simulator connection and on a single-command EthernetASCII message, instead of changing the controller's factor silently and leaving the SDK's scaling cache stale. The rejection now also covers a spaced form (APosUnitFct =0.5 — the controller reads it as the same write) and fires before the value is validated, so a malformed or out-of-range config write reports 4023 rather than a value error. The AACommMessage.AllowUserUnitsConfig bypass is unchanged. CommAPI.OnUserUnitsEnabledChanged and the ack-authoritative enabled cache now also follow a UserUnitsEn write sent as a MessageType.EthernetASCII message, and one written with spaces around the assignment (AUserUnitsEn =1); both were missed, so toggling units that way left CommAPI.GetUserUnitsEnabled reporting the old state and no event raised. Recording-parameter download no longer risks scaling the trigger value twice. TriggerContainer de-scales RecTrigVal / RecTrigValMax when it is built, and AACommDataRecManager now sends the parameter batch with the per-message User Units opt-out, so the value crosses exactly as the trigger computed it. User Units scaling no longer keeps the pre-reboot factors after a controller reset. The scaling configuration is read from the controller at Connect; a reset the session survives — sync SendReceive or async Send of MessageType.ResetRequest — now re-reads it, so a controller that comes back on a different *UnitFct or UserUnitsEn is scaled by its new values instead of the stale ones. A reset that returns an error leaves the cached configuration untouched. The re-read is synchronous: it completes before a sync SendReceive returns, and for an async reset it runs after the recovery wait and before the reply callback. Numbers now cross the AAComm boundary in the invariant culture in both directions. On a comma-decimal locale (German, French, most of continental Europe) the SDK formatted values in the process culture while parsing them back invariantly, so a User Units factor or a recording-trigger value of 0.01 went to the controller as 0,01 and was read there as 1 — a hundredfold-wrong value accepted with no error — and ParamAbout bounds in the controller's own About data threw FormatException, failing the connect. Reply text changes shape on those locales: a scaled reply, an AllStat value and a ParamAbout bound now read 0.01, not 0,01. The text is also exact and stable — it parses back to the very value that produced it, and is byte-identical on .NET Framework 4.8, .NET 8 and .NET 10, where the previous rendering was 15-digit lossy on .NET Framework only. Integral wire tokens go invariant too: on a locale whose negative sign is U+2212 (Swedish, Finnish, Norwegian, Estonian, Lithuanian) a negative controller value used to lose its sign on .NET 8/10 and arrive positive. FirmwareVersionStr and FPGAVersionStr follow, so a legacy controller now reports 4.123 rather than 4,123 — a .cup user-program file written on a comma-decimal machine before this change still downloads, its stored version being normalised before the compatibility check. A consumer parsing an AAComm reply must parse it with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture. Controller-FPGA download (.dat, AACommDownloadFPGA) to an EtherCAT drive over Ethernet no longer strands mid-flash. After the password handshake the process unconditionally reconnected at the factory default 172.1.1.101 — but an EtherCAT drive keeps its own address in FPGA-download mode, so nothing answered there and the download failed with Failed reconnecting in boot mode while the drive waited in download mode. The reconnect now targets the address the product actually comes up on (EtherCAT: its own; legacy: the factory default, as before), with the other address as fallback. Controller-FPGA download (.dat, AACommDownloadFPGA) no longer raises OnProgress after the OnProcessEnded that ends its download. The progress it reports while the controller finalizes the flash stopped only once it found the instance idle, so a tick could arrive after OnProcessEnded, and a download started on the same instance from OnProcessEnded kept receiving that ramp mixed into its own progress. Each download now stops its own finalize progress, and waits for an OnProgress call still running to return, before it raises OnProcessEnded. Firmware download to a legacy or EtherCAT controller over Ethernet no longer fails intermittently with Failed reconnecting Ethernet ... AACommServerNotRunning (14.0.0 regression). The controller drops its link on the way into BOOT, the bundled AACommServer fatal-evicts the downloader — its only client — and, since 14.0.0, that client's socket closing ended the server before the downloader could reconnect to the boot image. The server now keeps a five-second grace window after its last client dies (sized by rig experiment — the reconnect goes straight to the boot image's known address and returns well inside it): a client that opens a channel within the window keeps the server up; otherwise it exits as before. AGM800 (.bin) and RS-232 downloads never reconnect and were unaffected. The window lives in the bundled server, so client and sidecar must move together: a new client against a 14.0.0 AACommServer.exe still loses the race. Reported parameter bounds now match the units the value itself comes back in. ParamAbout scaled its min/max/default by the factor of ParamAbout — never by the factor of the parameter being asked about — so bounds came back in counts while the value came back in units; they now carry the queried parameter's factor. The same bounds (the parameter-info description and the "Allowed range" text on an out-of-range error) also ignored the per-axis User Units enable state and were reported in units on an axis that had them switched off; they now report counts until the axis enables units, and likewise while the consumer-wide CommAPI.SkipUserUnits is set. AACommMessage.SkipUserUnits now really covers AAllStat replies, as documented. The AllStat reply path re-read the API-wide CommAPI.SkipUserUnits instead, so a single raw-units query was silently scaled anyway. Related: on a controller without 64-bit AllStat support the raw AllStat reply was handed back completely unscaled, so an axis in user units read in mm through APos but in counts through AAllStat; those replies are now scaled like every other one. A reply that is not a numeric AllStat vector of the length the axes/groups masks describe — an ERR nn reply above all — is passed through untouched, so a controller error still reads as an error. AACommDownloadFW: firmware download to a legacy (non-AGM800, non-EtherCAT) controller over Ethernet now completes from a non-default address. The legacy boot image comes up on the factory default 172.1.1.101 regardless of the application's address, and the download used to fail at "Failed reconnecting Ethernet" while retrying the original one; after the flash erase it now reconnects at the default address first, and at the original address if a boot image kept it (the existing guard that refuses the download while another device owns the default address is unchanged). After the download the controller reboots on its own address. AllStatData.IsParsedOK now reports a failed AllStat parse instead of hiding it. A field that is not a number — a controller ERR nn reply above all — was read with a discarded TryParse and stored as 0 while IsParsedOK stayed true, so a bad reply looked like a wall of valid zero readings; it now sets IsParsedOK to false. Fields are read in the invariant culture, matching the way the reply is written. AACommDownloadUP.DownloadUserProgram reports a rejected request through OnProcessEnded instead of never completing. A call that is refused before the download starts — a disconnected or null CommAPI, or a user-program path that does not exist — raised its refusal on a background task nothing observed, because the exclusive-comms teardown dereferenced the controller handle the refused call had never taken; the callback that reports the outcome never fired. A consumer waiting on it saw no error text and waited out its own timeout, or waited indefinitely where it had none. The refusal now arrives as the callback's error description (API not connected, Invalid user program file), and runs no exclusive-comms teardown at all: a call that never took a controller handle no longer reaches for the one a previous call on the same instance left behind. AACommDownloadFPGARemote.StartDownloading no longer disconnects a CommAPI the refused call did not connect. Every refusal — a null argument, an out-of-range port, an API that is already connected (AAComm must be disconnected!), a non-AGM800 product, a channel other than Ethernet — ran the same teardown as a failed download, so on an instance that had already flashed once it disconnected the API of the previous call, and a caller that handed in a live connection to be told to disconnect it first had it dropped for them. A refusal now only reports through OnProcessEnded. A failure after this call's own Connect succeeded still disconnects the connection it opened, so the documented end state (API disconnected, success or error) is unchanged for a call that got that far. AACommDownloadFPGA, AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat and AACommDownloadFW disconnect the connection they opened when a check fails after their own connect succeeded. A controller whose firmware does not implement FPGA download or whose boot version is too old, an unreadable .dat / .ver / .hex file, an FPGA file for another product, an FW/FPGA version mismatch, a firmware file whose target does not match, another AAComm client on the controller — each reported through OnProcessEnded and left the CommAPI connected, so a caller that did not disconnect it itself was refused on its next attempt (AAComm must be disconnected!, AAComm is connected. Disconnect, and try again.). Each engine's documented end state (API disconnected, success or error) now holds for those failures too. A refusal raised before the connect still touches no CommAPI: that connection is the caller's own. AACommDownloadFW.StartDownloadingSafe refuses a call made while a download is already running on the instance (FW Download is already in progress!) before the pre-flight checks run. The currents verification (verifyCurrentRatings: true) connects to the controller, reads AIdentity[10] and AIdentity[9] and disconnects — and it ran first, on the API the running download owns and reconnects several times, so the refused call took the controller away mid-flash and reported a current-rating mismatch or a connection failure instead of the refusal. AACommDownloadFW.StartDownloading refuses a null api or connData through OnProcessEnded (Invalid input argument: CommAPI, Invalid input argument: ConnectionData), the texts StartDownloadingSafe reports for the same arguments, without the Error: prefix its catch-all adds. A null connData threw a NullReferenceException out of the call, and a null api was accepted: the instance marked itself busy, started its worker and reported the resulting NullReferenceException message as the download's outcome. An AACommDownloadUP.DownloadUserProgram call refused because another download is still running on the same instance (Download is already in process!) no longer disturbs that download. The refusal ended the running download's exclusive-communication session and marked the instance idle while the transfer continued, and a refusal that arrived while the running download was still waiting for exclusive access stopped it from ever starting, so its outcome was never reported. The refusal now only reports through OnProcessEnded. That callback is shared by every call on the instance, so the running download's handler also receives the refusal text, in no guaranteed order relative to its own result.
