AACommDownloadFPGARemote.StartDownloading refuses a second call the same way (Remote FPGA Download is already in progress!), where it disconnected the CommAPI of the flash in progress. An AACommDataRecManager call refused because an operation is already running on the same instance (Async operation in progress!) no longer marks that instance idle. The refusal cleared the running operation's in-progress flag, so the next call was accepted while the first was still driving the controller: the two then shared the CommAPI the manager holds and the completion callback it fires, and the first operation's completion invoked the later caller's. Every entry point refused this way — SendRecordingParams, StartRecording, ForceTrigger, StopRecording, WaitForRecToEnd, UploadRecData, UploadRecDataNonblocking. A refused StartRecording, ForceTrigger or StopRecording also replaced the parameter resolver the running operation sends its commands through, because that resolver was built before the call was refused; it is now built only once the call has been accepted. The same ordering means a null api passed to those three threw a NullReferenceException out of the call, since the resolver was built from it before the argument was checked; all three now report Invalid input argument: API is null through OnError, as their documentation already promised. The refusal now only reports through OnError. That callback is shared by every call on the instance, so the running operation's handler also receives the refusal text, in no guaranteed order relative to its own result. AACommDataRecManager.CancelUpload ends the operation that holds the instance instead of releasing the instance and abandoning that operation. It cleared the in-progress flag whatever was running, while cancelling only a sequential UploadRecDataNonblocking upload: a WaitForRecToEnd kept polling RecStat and a blocking UploadRecData stayed in flight, their caller told nothing, and the next call — accepted because the flag was clear — took over the same instance's CommAPI, parameter resolver and completion callback, so the abandoned operation's reply invoked the later caller's. A cancel now reports Operation cancelled through OnError, which is how the running operation's caller learns it ended; it cancels a sequential upload and stops the RecStat poll between queries; and a cancel with nothing running does nothing, where it used to clear an already-clear flag. A caller that expected CancelUpload to be silent now receives one OnError for the operation it cancelled. A request already on the wire is not recalled - a command, a parameter batch, a blocking upload or a RecStat query in flight still gets its reply - but a reply that arrives after the cancel is discarded: it re-arms no poll, sends no further parameter, runs no completion and releases nothing. A reply already being handled when the cancel runs is not interrupted. Global User Units now arm on a connection whose channel cannot carry a bulk (RS-232, CAN, the legacy Simulator channel). The group/factor/units configuration read and the sanctioned ControllerMessagesContainer.TrySetUnitsSync write batched their commands into a MessageType.BulkMessage, which AAComm refuses outside Ethernet with PC Suite: ERR 4004 — so the read failed at connect, UserUnitsSupported stayed false for the rest of the session, every factor resolved to 1 and nothing was scaled on those transports, with no error surfaced to the caller. Both paths now send one message per command where the channel cannot batch, so support, per-axis enable, factors and unit names come off the wire and scaling works over RS-232 and CAN. TrySetUnitsSync writes over RS-232 as it does over Ethernet; over CAN it now reports ErrorWritingData when the controller declares *UnitFct as a double, because a 64-bit assignment does not fit a CAN frame (error 304, a pre-existing limitation of that channel) — the write fails loudly with the cached factor left describing the controller, where a partial write used to report success. The single-message path also keeps the bulk's halt-on-error contract: nothing is sent after a command the controller (or the transmit path) refuses. Channels that carry a bulk — Ethernet and Simulation — still send the single bulk, unchanged. A process that starts the AACommServer no longer leaves its own output open behind it. The spawned server is shared and outlives the process that started it, and it held that process's stdout and stderr, so a caller reading them — a script piping a tool, a CI step capturing its log to a file — waited for the server to exit after the work had finished. On Windows the server is now started through the shell with a hidden window, so it inherits none of the starter's handles; elsewhere it gets its own standard streams. A console server host (AACommServerNative, or a managed server run through dotnet) spawned on Windows now has its own hidden console, so a Ctrl+C in the starter's console no longer reaches it; CloseAACommServer still stops it. Two calls that arrive together on one download engine no longer both take the download. AACommDownloadUP, AACommDownloadFW, AACommDownloadFPGA, AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat and AACommDownloadFPGARemote read their in-progress flag on entry and set it several statements later, so two threads could both pass the check: both then ran, each overwriting per-download state the other had just stored - the CommAPI in every engine, and the file and connection data in those that keep them, and neither was told it was refused. Each engine now takes the flag in one atomic step at entry and releases it on every path that does not start a download, so exactly one call proceeds and the other gets that engine's existing refusal text through OnProcessEnded — Download is already in process!, FW Download is already in progress!, FPGA Download is already in progress!, Remote FPGA Download is already in progress!. AACommDownloadFW.StartDownloadingSafe holds the flag across its currents pre-flight, so a call arriving while that pre-flight runs is refused instead of admitted. A caller that starts one download at a time sees no change. Two calls that arrive together on one AACommDataRecManager no longer both take the instance. The manager read its in-progress flag on entry and set it a few statements later, inside the pre-operation validation, so two calls could both pass the check: both then ran on the one manager, each overwriting the CommAPI, the parameter resolver and the completion callback the other had just stored, and neither was told it was refused - so one operation's reply invoked the other caller's completion. Every entry point is affected: SendRecordingParams, StartRecording, ForceTrigger, StopRecording, WaitForRecToEnd, UploadRecData and UploadRecDataNonblocking. The flag is now taken in one atomic step at entry and released on every path that does not start an operation, so exactly one call proceeds and the other gets Async operation in progress! through OnError, as a call refused for an already-running operation does. A caller that starts one operation at a time sees no change. The AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat.OnProgress documentation now states the scale the event reports, percent (0 to 100); it said fractions of 1000. The values the event reports are unchanged. AACommDownloadFPGARemote and AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat refuse an empty image, or one whose length is not a whole number of 4-byte words, before connecting, where they used to erase the FPGA's primary image and write only its whole words, so a partial last word was lost and an image under 4 bytes wrote nothing. OnProcessEnded reports Invalid input argument: FPGA image length must be a non-zero multiple of 4 bytes (got <length>), and nothing is sent to the controller. AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat refuses a null image the same way, reporting Invalid input argument: FPGA image. With the packet sniffer on, a controller connecting over Ethernet no longer waits on the sniffer's session lock just to record the capture task it started. A slow Npcap device open holds that lock, so the server's handling of the new channel could stall for the length of the open. AACommRemoteFpgaInfo.VariantStr shows the variant from the .ver file; it showed NA whenever the amplifier version was NA. VariantStr, AmpVersionStr and CommVersionStr print their value as upper-case hex behind 0x, as it is written in the .ver file; they printed the decimal digits, so 0x1D01 showed as 0x7425. A value of 0 shows NA. The binary continuous-integer replies (AxSt; and V1AxSt; AllStat and ParamAbout, V1RecUpload; recording upload) over Ethernet or a firmware simulation end only on a > that closes a whole number of 5-byte (32-bit) or 9-byte (64-bit) segments, or that follows less than one segment. They used to end on any read whose last byte was >, so a 0x3E inside a 64-bit value could cut the reply short at a read boundary. The legacy forms (RecUploadOK;, RecUpload;, AxisStatusOK;) still end on the last byte. A firmware simulation is configured on connect unless its AMotorType query is answered with a plain non-zero value; an error or malformed reply used to read as "already configured" and left the simulated motor unconfigured. The commutation recipe now goes to axes A to L, not only axis A (an error from an axis the simulation does not have is skipped); a SimMotorProfile with [A]..[L] sections gives an axis its own encoder resolution and pole pairs, and [global] / [all] open the block every axis starts from. ARPTools.LookupResult.DoesIpv4SubnetMatch and ARPTools.EthernetLookupResults.IsSubnetSetOnAny match a subnet on whole octets. They compared a bare text prefix, so subnet 172.1.1 also matched an adapter at 172.1.10.x, 172.1.11.x or 172.1.100.x to 172.1.199.x. An Ethernet connect to a 172.1.1.x controller from a PC whose adapters sit only on such an address now fails with EthernetInterfaceMismatch, as it does for any other subnet, instead of going on to ping the controller from no adapter on its subnet. A throwing OnProcessEnded handler no longer gets a second, failure report from AACommDownloadFPGA, AACommDownloadFPGARemote and AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat: the handler is called once, with the true outcome of the download, and the connection is disconnected and the instance released once. AACommDownloadFPGARemote.StartDownloading with a null fpgaInfo reports Invalid input argument: AACommRemoteFpgaInfo through OnProcessEnded instead of the runtime's NullReferenceException text. AACommRemoteFpgaInfo(string rpdFile) finds the .ver beside a relative .rpd path such as amp.rpd, which it refused, and on Linux and macOS finds it for any path, which it always refused. ARPTools.EthernetLookupResults.GetSubnetMismatchString on an empty lookup returns its text with NA for the adapter and its address instead of throwing ArgumentOutOfRangeException. A disconnect closes its IPC socket to AACommServer even when AACommServer has already dropped the connection, instead of leaving the socket open until garbage collection. AACommFwInfo refuses each firmware-file mismatch with one text, whether its constructor or ValidateFwFiles refuses it: a non-.bin file for an AGM800 reads Only '.bin' files can be flashed to AGM800 products, and a .bin for a product that takes .hex files reads <product> can be flashed with '.hex' files only. ValidateFwFiles worded both differently. AACommDownloadFPGA and AACommDownloadFPGAEtherCat raise OnProcessEnded only once the controller accepts a connection again after the reset that ends the download, so a handler may reconnect at once. A controller that does not answer within 60 seconds ends the download with an error. AACommDownloadFPGA no longer waits a fixed 6 seconds instead Deprecated ConnectResult.FwInfoMismatch — Connect no longer returns it. [14.0.0] - 2026-08-26 ⚠️ Breaking AAComm.dll is now strong-named (PublicKeyToken=043a10799a9b732b), so strong-named consumers can reference it — previously they compiled with warning CS8002 and failed at load with FileLoadException 0x80131044: A strongly-named assembly is required. Adding the strong name changes the assembly identity: .NET Framework consumers must recompile against 14.0.0 (a binary built against a 13.x AAComm, PublicKeyToken=null reference does not bind to the signed assembly, and no binding redirect bridges an identity change); .NET 8/10 consumers see no difference. The AssemblyVersion is pinned to 14.0.0.0 for the whole 14.x line (package and file version keep the full number), so a consumer built against 14.0.0 binds to any 14.x without redirects. Persisted assembly-qualified type names that spell PublicKeyToken=null (e.g. BinaryFormatter payloads, Type.GetType full-name strings) stop resolving — simple names (AAComm.CommAPI, AAComm) are unaffected. AACommServerCore.dll (bundled with the server) is signed too; the AACommServer.exe process itself is not — see docs/strong-naming.md in the repo for the assembly-by-assembly map and the reason. The C++/CLI AACommNative wrapper has been retired (with its AACommNativeTester/AACommNativeTesterCLI projects). The NuGet no longer ships the lib/cppCLI/net48/ slot (IAACommNative.h, AACommNative.lib/.dll, shared sources). Native (C/C++) consumers move to the new C-ABI SDK — project AACommNative (reclaiming the name) → aacomm.h + aacomm.dll/libaacomm.so/libaacomm.dylib. OnResetProgress replaced by two events — OnLongOperationStarted(LongOperationType) and OnLongOperationEnded(LongOperationType, int errorCode) — now firing for Reset, Save, Load, SaveUser, and EventCorrect. The ended edge's errorCode is 0 on success or the controller error code (e.g. 22 = "motor on") on failure, so subscribers can suppress a "complete" message on a failed long operation (issue #85). For the non-Reset types, a reply that arrives within a short start-grace window (100 ms) raises neither edge — an immediately-rejected operation (e.g. ERR 22 declining a flash Save while the motor is on) is not long-running, so no transient "started" notification can race and overwrite the error the reply itself reports. Subscribers must update their handler signatures. The native C-ABI SDK mirrors this with aacomm_set_longop_started_callback / aacomm_set_longop_ended_callback. Binary IPC dialect v3 — typed payloads: binary requests now carry a typed message kind plus the raw payload bytes instead of ASCII-rendered, prefix-tagged strings, removing a redundant render/parse on both ends of every message. Measured on AGM800 and AGD301, binary round-trips now match or beat the ASCII protocol (previously ~15 % slower) with materially tighter tail latencies. The dialect is negotiated at connect: a version-skewed binary peer — old client on a new server, or new client on an old server — degrades to the ASCII compat protocol; the previous binary dialect is removed. The AACommServer comm log keeps showing the readable command text (carried alongside the binary payload for display); FW/UP download payloads log masked as binary, as before. CommAPI now negotiates the wire protocol with AACommServer at connect time — binary by default, falling back to the legacy ASCII protocol when the server is an old ASCII-only build. The fallback is no longer silent: CommAPI.ServerCompat (see Added) reports the attached server's classification, so hosts can warn the user. The consumer does not select the protocol — new CommAPI() remains the only construction, and the negotiated mode is reported by CommAPI.Protocol (see Added). The ASCII client pipeline is deprecated and frozen — kept solely for compat with servers started by older SDK applications. IChannelSnifferHook.OnChannelClosed(bool) is now OnChannelClosed(SnifferConnectionInfo connectionInfo, bool isError) — the close notification carries the controller endpoint so a host capturing several controllers at once can route the snapshot to the right NIC. Host sniffer integrations must update the signature. AACommAxisHelper is merged into the new AAComm.Services.AACommMnemonicHelper (see Added) and removed. AAxis, PAxis, ToAxis, ToAxisIdx(char) and ToAxisChar are unchanged and live in the same namespace, so their extension call sites recompile as-is; direct class-name references (AACommAxisHelper.AAxis → AACommMnemonicHelper.AAxis) need updating. Two redundant members are dropped: ToAxisStr(int) (use ToAxis(idx).ToString()) and the ToAxisIdx(string) overload (use s.ToAxisChar().ToAxisIdx() — makes the first-char truncation explicit). AACommMessage.StartsWithPAxis(string) removed — use msg.ToAxisChar() == AACommMnemonicHelper.PAxis (identical semantics, including null/empty → false). LoggerDataContainer / ScopeDataContainer constructors take a new required char[] parameter (paramAxes / signalAxes — the per-vector axis letters, needed to resolve User-Units scaling per axis) in addition to the CommAPI→ICommService narrowing. Existing call sites must supply the axis array. TriggerContainer construction is reshaped into three overloads: by source CCC code (ICommService, int trigType, int trigSrcCCC, …), by source mnemonic (ICommService, int trigType, string trigParam, …), or source-less (int trigType, double trigVal, …) for triggers that carry no parameter source. The previous single-constructor call sites must pick the matching overload. MessageData.DefaultValueStr (deprecated in 11.1.0 with its Min/Max siblings) is removed with the rest of that property group; its replacement lives on MessageDataValueExtensions like the others (see Added). The native C-ABI SDK (aacomm.*) adopts a uniform status convention: every aacomm_* function now returns int32_t aacomm_status (AACOMM_OK=0 / AACOMM_NULL_ARG=-1 / AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE=-2 / AACOMM_EXCEPTION=-3), and domain results (the ConnectResult, the connected flag, reply/error byte sizes) move to out_* parameters. So aacomm_create, aacomm_destroy, aacomm_is_connected, aacomm_last_error, aacomm_start_server, aacomm_test_connection, aacomm_connect/_silent, aacomm_send_receive, and aacomm_last_reply all change signature (e.g. aacomm_create(aacomm_handle* out), aacomm_is_connected(h, int32_t* out_connected)) — this removes the old ambiguity where aacomm_is_connected returned 0 for both "not connected" and a bad handle. Handles now come from a table that rejects forged/stale/double-freed handles with AACOMM_BAD_HANDLE instead of risking undefined behavior. Adds aacomm_close_server(h, force) to shut down a spawned AACS. ABI generation resets to 1 at first ship under the soname policy (the ABI number now bumps only on breaking changes; additive growth never bumps it — see the AACommNative README); native consumers rebuild against the shipped aacomm.h. XmlHandler.SaveXml() is removed in favour of TrySaveXml(out Exception) (see Added). It returned nothing and reported a failed write only through a Debug.Assert — a no-op in Release, so a document that never reached disk passed silently. Added Always-on client diagnostic log — AAComm.Services.Diagnostics.AACommDebugLog, the client-side counterpart of AACommServer's debug log. Session-lifecycle events (construction, connect/test outcomes, sync-timeout expiries — including the phase-1 queue-abandon vs phase-2 teardown distinction — server FATALs, disconnects with their reason) accumulate in an in-memory ring with zero configuration and zero steady-state file IO; a severe event (sync phase-2 teardown, FATAL, comms error) snapshots the ring to %LocalAppData%\PCSuite\AAComm_DebugLogs\{timestamp}_{process}_{pid}_{trigger}.log (debounced, pruned at 200 files). Every line carries an identity tag (api#N/conn#M); the connect line logs the endpoint and the socket's local port, which joins against the UserId ↔ client-endpoint line AACommServer now writes on each Open. Public surface: AACommDebugLog.Sink (an Action<string,string> bridge so hosts can forward the lines into their own log) and AACommDebugLog.Flush() (on-demand snapshot). Full spec: docs/diagnostics-srs.md. User Units — per-axis engineering-unit scaling, applied transparently to parameter values on both send and receive. At connect, the API reads the controller's units configuration (the *UnitGroup/*UnitFct/*UnitUnt parameter families, grouped per UUGroups: Pos/PosAux/PosPD/Vel/VelAux/VelPD/Acc/Frc) and the per-axis UserUnitsEn enables; from then on values of parameters in an enabled group are scaled by the axis factor in both directions. The new AAComm.Services.UserUnits namespace carries the model (UserUnitGroup, UserUnitAxis, UserUnitsData, UUGroups, UUErrors, UUMnemonics). The surface: CommAPI: GetUserUnitsEnabled(char) / SetUserUnitsEnabled(char, bool) (per-axis query/enable — the setter is controller-ack-authoritative), RefreshUserUnits() (re-read the configuration), OnUserUnitsEnabledChanged (raised on a confirmed per-axis transition), and SkipUserUnits (consumer-wide bypass, reset to false at Connect). AACommMessage: SkipUserUnits (per-message bypass) and AllowUserUnitsConfig (sanctions a raw write of the units-config parameters themselves — without it such writes are rejected with ERR 4023; set units through TrySetUnitsSync instead), plus constructor overloads taking skipUserUnits. ControllerMessagesContainer: UserUnitsSupported, MaxUserUnitNameLen(UUGroups), TryGetUserUnitAxis/TryGetUserUnitsGroup (read-only lookups, also on IMessagesContainer — implementors must add them), and TrySetUnitsSync(ICommService, UUGroups, char, string, double) — the sanctioned, synchronous write of a group's units name + factor. MessageData: UserUnits (the parameter's group, read-only), GetUserUnitsData(char) returning a UserUnitsData struct (Min/Max/Default scaled for the axis + Factor/Units), and GetDescription(char) (the parameter description with per-axis units resolved). FloatHelper: ApplyUserUnits/RemoveUserUnits — the Rx/Tx scaling primitives, for consumers formatting values outside a message flow. ICommService exposes GetUserUnitsEnabled(char). The native C-ABI SDK mirrors the per-axis enable/query as aacomm_get_user_units_enabled/aacomm_set_user_units_enabled. AAComm.Services.AACommMnemonicHelper — the SDK home for controller-message string manipulation, consolidating helpers previously spread across host-side libraries. Covers axis-letter conversions (absorbed from AACommAxisHelper), the '?' active-axis / '*' all-axes sentinels, mnemonic extraction (Mnemonic, SplitMessage), array-index handling (ArrayIndex, SeparateArrayIndex, RemoveArrayIndex), assignment/equality location that skips comparison operators (IndexOfEquality, IndexOfAssignment, IndexOfMnemonicEnd). IsAxisInRange(char, IIdentityContainer) validates an axis letter against the connected controller's actual axis count (the dynamic 'P' axis is always valid; disconnected falls back to the theoretical 12-axis 'A'–'L' range). MessageData value accessors (MinValueStr/MaxValueStr/DefaultValueStr, MinValueInt/MaxValueInt/DefaultValueInt, MinValueLong/MaxValueLong/DefaultValueLong) — extension methods on MessageDataValueExtensions formatting Min/Max/Default per the parameter type (no User-Units scaling), replacing the host-side equivalents that backed the properties deprecated in 11.1.0. IIdentityContainer exposes Features_02, CurrentLoopSampleRate, MaxNumOfRecVectors, MaxDataRecordingPoints, NumOfMotorAxes — needed by Core consumers of the recording pipeline and the User Units API. IMessagesContainer exposes Contains(string), CanCodeToData, IsInitialized; ICommService exposes MessagesInBulk. Implementors of these interfaces must add the members. Recording-pipeline command builders are now public API: TriggersDataContainer.GetDownloadCommands(RecParamsResolver) / TriggerContainer.GetDownloadCommands(RecParamsResolver, int) (the trigger setup commands a recording download sends) and RecParamsResolver.GetTriggerIndex / GetTriggerLogicIndex (slot resolution for trigger sources) — needed by host recording tools driving the pipeline through the abstractions. Binary IPC protocol v2 (additive, version-safe both directions): every request carries a correlation id the server echoes on its reply, and the client routes replies by identity instead of arrival order — eliminating a class of cross-flow reply misrouting when Send and SendReceive run concurrently (server-internal queries could previously overtake a pending controller reply and each caller received the other's answer). Legacy servers/clients interoperate unchanged (id 0 keeps arrival-order routing). A new CHANNEL_EVENT reply kind — sent only to clients that declare support on Open — notifies a passive client when its channel dies; it surfaces via OnCommsError. The bundled AACommServer packet sniffer now captures every connected controller simultaneously — one capture session, ring buffer, and snapshot tree per controller endpoint (under per-NIC ip_port subfolders) — instead of only the most-recently-opened channel's NIC. The server window lists a live status/packet row per controller with per-NIC Mark and Export. CommAPI and AACommServerModel now implement IDisposable — Dispose() delegates to Disconnect() / Shutdown() respectively, so consumers can use using blocks. CommAPI.Dispose() does not shut down the shared AACommServer process (call CloseAACommServer() for that); both are idempotent. CommAPI.FlushDebugLog() — asks the attached AACommServer to write its in-memory debug log to disk now, instead of only at server shutdown, so a support snapshot taken while the problem is happening captures the current session rather than the previous one. Works whether or not the caller is connected, does not clear the server's log or disturb a running session, and is a no-op when no server is running. It is fire-and-forget — there is no acknowledgement: the result is the newest {yyyy_MM_dd_HH-mm-ss}_Flush.log under %LocalAppData%\PCSuite\AACommServer_DebugLogs. Available on both the binary and legacy ASCII wire protocols; against an older AACommServer the request is ignored. CommAPI.Protocol (new ProtocolMode enum: Ascii/Binary) — read-only report of the wire protocol negotiated with AACommServer (valid after Connect). CommAPI.ServerCompat (new ServerCompat enum: Unknown/Current/LegacyBinary/LegacyAscii) — classification of the AACommServer the client attached to, valid after Connect. The version floor classifies, it never rejects: an old server started by an older SDK application still serves this client in compat mode (it owns the shared port; a client never shuts down a server it did not spawn), but the degraded mode — arrival-order routing on ASCII, missing channel events, skipped version-gated features — is now queryable instead of silent. The server now reports its version in 3-part major.minor.patch form. The package now also ships a net10.0 target (alongside net48 and net8.0) — .NET 10 is the current LTS runtime; net8.0 reaches end of support 2026-11. .NETCoreApp consumers on either runtime get the same native AACS sidecar. Ethernet connections to loopback addresses (127.x) are now accepted — enables connecting to a PC-hosted firmware simulation without a physical network adapter. ChannelType.Simulation — new managed firmware-sim channel. AACommServer launches a local firmware_sim process over loopback and bridges it, presenting a real moving plant. Replaces the legacy ChannelType.Simulator for end-to-end simulation — that param-echo channel's server backend is removed; the Simulator enum is retained only for AAComm's in-process virtual-test harness. The child process is spawned on connect and reaped on close. ConnectionData.SimExePath / SimProduct / SimVersion / SimMotorProfile — configure the managed Simulation channel (the firmware_sim executable to launch plus its catalog identity and motor profile). ConnectResultInterpreter.Interpret(ConnectResult) now returns localized text (en-US / zh-CN) per LocaleProvider.Instance.Locale. XmlHandler.TrySaveXml(out Exception) — saves the document, returning false with the failure that stopped the final attempt when it could not be written after ten retries. Replaces SaveXml() (see Breaking). Four new ConnectResult codes: CANDeviceNotConnected (48) — a CAN Connect found the Kvaser driver installed but no physical Kvaser interface connected (canlib enumerates only virtual channels; distinct from CANLibMissing, the driver itself absent — the native C-ABI SDK exposes it as AACOMM_RESULT_CANDEVICE_NOT_CONNECTED); SimLaunchFailed (49) / SimNoPort (50) — the managed Simulation channel's firmware_sim process could not be launched / did not announce its loopback port; and ServerNotBinaryCapable (47) — an internal protocol-negotiation signal (a binary Open that got no handshake ack), never returned from a public Connect. Fixed Connect and TestConnection no longer fail on a busy machine while the controller is healthy. Both steps of the connect handshake were budgeted as if they measured controller response time, but each depended on ThreadPool scheduling, so CPU pressure — a build, a test run, another application — could produce AACommServerNotRunning against a server that was listening, or FailControllerType against a controller answering in under a millisecond. Three changes: the server-liveness probe completes its loopback check on the calling thread instead of waiting on a pool-dispatched completion; a message waiting to reach the wire is no longer charged that wait against its own TimeoutMs when nothing else is on the wire, since only client-side scheduling can delay it there; and a dispatched request is no longer torn down for delays that are not the controller's — client-side completion scheduling, or server-side queueing behind another client — the synchronous wait grants starvation headroom above TimeoutMs + 100 before implicating the link, because the server itself polices controller silence at TimeoutMs and reports it as a FATAL. A genuinely unresponsive server is still detected and disconnected, a few seconds later than before. A message queued behind a live one keeps its caller's budget and stays as responsive as before, and TimeoutMs still means what it always did to the server — the controller's reply budget — so a wedged controller is still detected promptly. Measured against a live controller on a 12-core host: the first two changes took connect failures under load from reproducible to rare cold-start-only cases, and the third targets that remainder; idle-path latency unchanged. AACommFwInfo now reads the identity block (product, version, current ratings, identity text) of v5.x AGD301/AGD200 hex images. It located the block by counting records after the last 0x0014 segment record; those images fill that segment with code ahead of the block, so DataValid came back false, VerifyCurrents threw "selected FW file doesn't contain 'currents' information", and ValidateFwFiles skipped its product/version cross-checks. The block is now found by its record addresses; v3.x images and AGD155 read exactly as before. AACommServer no longer keeps a phantom channel user when a client's connection is reset while the server is still processing that client's request (an aborted connect, or a peer that dropped mid-request). The dead client stayed registered on its channel for the server's lifetime, so a later client on the same controller could be reported as one of several users and have its FW/FPGA download exclusivity check (NonSingleErr) refused until the server restarted. A push message whose payload legitimately ends in \r or > is no longer corrupted on the ASCII client path — the classifier used to strip all trailing framing characters instead of the single >\r framing pair, eating those payload bytes. The AACommServer's post-reset Ethernet reconnect now retries on a 30-second time budget instead of 5 fixed attempts. A controller that recovers slowly from AReset (11–17+ s observed on AGM800, during which the host link is also down) previously exhausted the attempts and fatally closed the channel ("Post-reset reconnect failed"); it now reconnects as soon as the controller returns. A controller still unreachable when the budget expires triggers the fatal teardown as before. AACommServer connect failures (including the post-reset reconnect FATAL) now report the concrete reason — e.g. Comms: EthernetFailARP (28) - Failed sending an ARP request to the controller IP — instead of the generic "Exception of type 'AACommServerCore.Comms.ConnectException' was thrown." text, in both the client-facing error and the server debug log. Ethernet discovery and connect now work on hosts with multiple NICs: ARP requests are sent from every local NIC whose subnet matches the target (previously SendARP used the OS "best-metric" interface only, so controllers behind other NICs were invisible to Discover, and a direct connect with an empty ARP table failed). Covers subnet discovery, the connect-path reachability check, and the FW/FPGA download ARP warm-ups. (issue #25) A controller reply over Ethernet consisting of only the RS232 terminator (>) with no value — a malformed/incomplete answer to a value query — now surfaces immediately as ERR 4024 instead of stalling until the channel times out and drops the connection. The server can tell it apart from a legitimate OK at the wire frame (a valid reply is [type-byte, …, '>']; the malformed one is a lone '>'), so no genuine reply is affected. (issue #45) 64-bit integer parameter assignments now transmit byte-exact. Every assignment was parsed through double (which carries only 2^53 of integer precision), so an int64 value above ~9·10^15 — e.g. one written verbatim to a .par file by a parameters upload — was silently rounded to a neighboring value on download/write. Plain-integer text now bypasses the double path when user units don't transform the value. AACommServer now honors Message and Close requests only from a socket whose open record names that channel (the membership gate). Previously a misbehaving client that never opened the channel — or sent a duplicate/stale Close — could latch exclusive comms on another client's channel (locking its members out and blocking ShutDownForce) or close the channel under its remaining users. UserProgVarsAdapter.AdaptUserProgMessage no longer drops the per-message User Units flags (SkipUserUnits, AllowUserUnitsConfig) when duplicating the message with adapted task/global-var names — a raw-units message routed through the adapter (e.g. every AAMotion synchronous command) was silently re-scaled, and a sanctioned UU-config write was self-blocked by the Tx-build gate. Spawning the bundled server is now robust across hosts and deployments: A spawned server is always started headless (--headless + redirected stdin) — a net8/native console consumer no longer gets the sidecar's Terminal.Gui monitoring TUI taking over its terminal (GUI apps no longer pop a console either). Started manually, the native host still opens its TUI; a second manual start now exits with a clear "port already in use" message instead of aborting. The spawn wait is a real deadline (15 s, sized to a cold-starting net48 WPF server) polling the port and detecting a child that died during startup — previously a fixed 500 ms grace made a slow cold start fail spuriously and leave an orphaned zero-client server behind. Server resolution probes the application base directory (where the package places the sidecar) before the working directory — a Windows-service host (cwd = System32) now finds its own sidecar. A .NET-Core client prefers AACommServerNative.exe, so a stale net48 AACommServer.exe left behind by an overlay upgrade can no longer be spawned into the old runtime-mismatch crash. The PCSuite-installation registry fallback reads the 32-bit registry view the installer actually writes — 64-bit net48 consumers previously missed an installed PCSuite entirely — and a present key with a missing InstallPath value reports the missing-installation result instead of an exception result. AACommServer's implicit last-client self-shutdown now also covers a client whose channel died under it: when a controller-link FATAL evicts a channel and its last client then disconnects, the server terminates as it does for any last-client death. Previously the fatal path erased the client's record first, so its death went unnoticed and a zero-client server lingered indefinitely — silently attached (whatever its version) by the next client to connect. A graceful Close still deliberately leaves the server running for reconnect flows. AACommServer: a repeated Open on the same client socket is now transactional — a re-Open that fails (unreachable target, disabled channel type) leaves the client's previous channel attachment fully intact. Previously the failure path released the previous membership and erased the client's open record up-front, orphaning the socket so the server's implicit last-client shutdown never triggered. A sole client re-Opening the same channel also no longer bounces the controller link through a momentarily-userless channel. A SendReceive whose timeout expires while the message is still queued behind a slower call no longer disconnects the whole API — it returns ERR Sync: Timeout and the message is never sent (previously a short-timeout call queued behind e.g. a 20 s MotorOn deterministically tore down the connection). The wire-timeout clock now starts when the message is dispatched, matching the server-enforced TimeoutMs; a timeout after the message reached the wire still disconnects, as before. An asynchronous Send callback now fires exactly once, even when the connection tears down (disconnect, controller-link FATAL) before the reply arrives — the in-flight message's callback gets ERR Sync: Session terminated and still-queued messages get PC Suite: ERR 4020, both with IsError set. Previously those callbacks were silently dropped, so a consumer waiting on the callback (e.g. a native-SDK / Python future) waited forever. One AAComm client can no longer stall or corrupt other clients sharing the AACommServer. The server's channel lifecycle was reworked so that slow operations — opening a channel to an unreachable controller, the post-Reset recovery wait, a reply to a client that stopped reading its socket — never block message routing for other clients or channels. Previously, one application connecting to a wrong IP could time out (and force-disconnect) another application's live session, a close during another client's Reset stalled the whole server for the recovery window, and a hung client could wedge its channel indefinitely. Each client socket also gets a dedicated ordered writer, so concurrent replies/pushes can never interleave frame bytes. When a hardware channel dies (controller link lost, timeout), every client of that channel is now notified — including passive clients with no request in flight, which previously discovered the death only when their next command failed. COMTools.GetFTDI_COMs() now lists the vendor-filtered (FTDI / Z-TEK / Prolific) USB-serial ports on net8.0 and native consumers — previously the WMI body was compiled out there (#if !NETCOREAPP), so those consumers got an empty list. Enumeration moved off WMI to the Windows registry (and udev /dev/serial/by-id on Linux), removing AAComm's last System.Management dependency. A failed or partial connection — or a channel FATAL racing an explicit Disconnect — is now reported as a proper ConnectResult instead of being masked by a NullReferenceException thrown from the connection-cleanup path while tearing down a not-yet-fully-open connection. A controller-link FATAL or sync-timeout that tears the connection down while a Connect/TestConnection is still mid-flight (reading controller identity) no longer NREs the in-flight connect. Connection teardown is now serialized on the connect lock, so the receive-thread FATAL handler can't dispose the handler out from under the connecting thread. Surfaced by connect/close churn against a saturated server. Rapidly closing a connection (tool-navigation churn) no longer emits a spurious comms error / debug assert from the binary-IPC receive loop racing the socket close — the disposed-socket teardown is now handled as the normal close it is. AACommServer no longer deadlocks when a client disconnects at the same moment one of its channels hits a FATAL timeout. A lock-order inversion between the channel registry and a channel's queue could wedge the server (hanging any connected client) until the process was killed. About-data parsing no longer overflows on ScalingFact values emitted as unsigned float bit patterns. Socket teardown no longer crashes the process on macOS/Linux hosts: connection-reset/abort detection now uses platform-normalized SocketErrorCode instead of the Windows-only raw error 10054 (affected both the binary and ASCII IPC clients). Connection-aborted, network-reset, and shutdown errors now also report the connection as lost instead of a generic error. A reply that fails inbound post-processing (e.g. a malformed ParamAbout answer) no longer tears down the whole session — conversion degrades to the raw reply string. Previously the exception unwound through the binary-IPC frame dispatch and every subsequent call failed with "PC Suite: ERR 4020". A controller link that dies mid-session (reset, cable pull, or clean remote close) now reliably surfaces as a connection-loss error and the API recovers with a plain reconnect. Previously a clean remote close left the channel half-dead (every command timing out individually), and the racing teardown paths could crash the host process. net8.0 / .NET-Core consumers received the net48 AACommServer.exe as their bundled server and crashed it on launch (a System.Runtime version mismatch when the net48 process loaded the consumer's net8.0 assemblies). Each consumer now gets a server matching its own runtime (see Changed). The net48 sidecar additionally ships its full runtime closure (it had been missing Google.Protobuf.dll). net8.0 / .NET-Core (and native C-ABI) clients could not connect over CAN — a client-side WMI Kvaser-presence pre-check was compiled out on .NET Core (#if !NETCOREAPP) and always reported "no device", so the connect failed with RequiredConnectionUnavailable before the (working) CAN transport was reached. The presence check now runs server-side via canlib (cross-platform, excluding virtual channels), so CAN connects succeed from net8.0 / native clients; when the host has no physical Kvaser interface the connect returns the new ConnectResult.CANDeviceNotConnected (see Added). Changed StartAACommServer now auto-locates a server on Linux and macOS (.NET 8/10 clients). It previously refused outright off Windows, so a non-Windows consumer had to pass an explicit path. The search is the application directory then the working directory, aacommserver/ before flat, looking for AACommServerNative — off Windows the NativeAOT host carries no extension and the net48 WPF host does not exist, so it is the only candidate. There is no install-location convention to fall back on, so a miss there is the final answer and still reports AACS_ResolveWrongOS, whose documentation now describes that rather than a blanket refusal. Windows resolution is unchanged, and .NET Framework clients keep their previous behaviour. The daemon's execute bit is restored before spawning it (Unix only). Neither a zip nor a NuGet package carries the Unix executable bit, so a host delivered through either arrives non-executable and the spawn failed with EACCES. Best-effort: a read-only mount or another owner's file is left alone, and the start reports the real error. A server host is launched directly unless it is a managed .dll. The launcher keyed off an .exe suffix, so the extensionless NativeAOT host on Linux/macOS was handed to dotnet as though it were an assembly. The release asset published to the public release page is now the Agito.AAComm.<version>.nupkg itself — the same package nuget.org serves. The AACommPackage_v.<version>.zip bundle is retired; its managed DLLs and server come from the NuGet package, and its DocFX copy of the API site is the site already published at https://akribis-agito.github.io/Agito-Releases/aacomm/. Non-.NET consumers keep the separate agito-aacomm-native-sdk-<version>.zip, which — with Agito.AAComm.Native.<version>.nupkg — now ships on its own public Software/AAComm-Native release line beside this one. The bundled net48 AACommServer closure now lands in an aacommserver\ subfolder of the consumer's output directory instead of flat at its root — the server's Google.Protobuf.dll and BCL shim DLLs no longer collide with the consumer's own same-name assemblies (the winner was previously decided by file timestamp). The server is resolved from the subfolder automatically; explicit StartAACommServer(path) calls and existing flat layouts keep working. A spawned (headless) net48 AACommServer that loses the socket-bind race — or finds the port blocked — now exits silently with a log entry instead of parking a modal retry dialog no one can dismiss; its spawner attaches to the winning instance. Interactive launches keep the dialog. AACommServer debug logs and packet-sniffer captures now live under %LOCALAPPDATA%\PCSuite\AACommServer_DebugLogs (was the Documents folder). Where Documents is OneDrive-redirected, sync locked the large rotating capture files and contended with the per-channel snapshot I/O; the local-app-data location is non-synced. The server's "Open Folder" button and log save-dialogs follow automatically. The per-snapshot total-size budget sweep is also throttled so connect/close churn doesn't re-walk the whole capture tree on every channel close. Firmware download over CAN is now explicitly rejected up front (AACommDownloadFW.StartDownloading/StartDownloadingSafe) with a clear message — "Firmware download is not supported over CAN. Download firmware over Ethernet (AGM800) or RS-232 (serial)." FW download was never functional over CAN (the controller-side CAN boot-loader FW-data contract is not met by this path); it previously failed mid-transfer with a cryptic controller error. Use Ethernet (AGM800) or RS-232. Removed the YamlDotNet dependency — the parameter-info and error-code databases are now build-generated; consumers no longer deploy YamlDotNet.dll. Internal: the bundled server-engine assembly was renamed AACommServerAPI.dll → AACommServerCore.dll (project AACommServerAPI → AACommServerCore). No public API change — consumers reference Agito.AAComm; only a consumer copying the engine DLL by name is affected. NuGet AACommServer sidecar selection is TFM-based (it was OS-based as of 12.1.1): .NETFramework consumers get the net48 WPF AACommServer.exe; .NETCoreApp (net8.0) consumers now get the self-contained NativeAOT AACommServerNative host (win-x64 — no .NET runtime on target; the same exe also runs a Terminal.Gui monitoring UI when launched interactively). Because the native exe carries no managed assemblies beside it, it resolves the prior net8-consumer crash where the consumer's own Google.Protobuf could shadow the server's. linux/osx net8 consumers have no sidecar until their native build runners land; consumers that need the WPF UI should target net48. The retired net8 AACommServerNetConsole + AACommServerNetAvalonia hosts are gone.
